/library/fibromyalgia.bodyHtml:
What is Fibromyalgia?

Fibromyalgia is a long-term condition that causes pain all over the body. It is one of the most common chronic pain conditions, affecting millions of people worldwide. Unlike some other pain conditions, fibromyalgia does not cause inflammation or damage to tissues and joints — instead, it affects the way the brain and nervous system process pain signals, making the body more sensitive to pain than normal.

The condition is more common in women than men, and it often develops in middle age, although it can affect anyone at any age, including children. Many people with fibromyalgia also have other conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), chronic fatigue syndrome, depression, and anxiety.

What Causes Fibromyalgia?

The exact cause of fibromyalgia is not fully understood, but researchers believe it is related to changes in the way the central nervous system processes pain messages. Some people develop fibromyalgia after a physical trauma such as a car accident, surgery, or an infection. Others experience the gradual onset of symptoms with no clear trigger.

There may also be a genetic component — fibromyalgia tends to run in families, suggesting that certain genes may make a person more vulnerable to developing it. Psychological stress and emotional trauma can also trigger or worsen symptoms in some people.

Symptoms

The main symptom of fibromyalgia is widespread pain throughout the body. However, the condition causes a wide range of other symptoms too:

  • Persistent, dull aching pain that lasts for at least three months
  • Extreme tiredness and fatigue, even after sleep
  • Sleep problems — difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep
  • Cognitive difficulties often called "fibro fog" — problems with memory, concentration, and thinking clearly
  • Headaches and migraines
  • Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)
  • Painful periods in women
  • Sensitivity to temperature, light, and sound
  • Restless leg syndrome
  • Numbness or tingling in hands and feet

How is it Diagnosed?

There is no specific test for fibromyalgia. Doctors diagnose it based on a patient's symptoms and by ruling out other conditions. Typically, a diagnosis is made when widespread pain has been present for more than three months and no other underlying condition explains it. Blood tests and imaging scans may be done to rule out other causes of pain, such as rheumatoid arthritis or lupus.

Treatment Options

While there is no cure for fibromyalgia, a combination of treatments can help manage symptoms and improve quality of life. Treatment is usually tailored to each person's specific symptoms and may include:

  • Medications — including painkillers, antidepressants (such as amitriptyline), and anticonvulsants
  • Exercise — gentle activities such as swimming, walking, and yoga have been shown to reduce pain and improve energy levels
  • Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) — talking therapy to help change the way you think about pain
  • Lifestyle changes — improving sleep habits, managing stress, and pacing activities
  • Complementary therapies — such as acupuncture, massage, and mindfulness

Living with Fibromyalgia

Living with fibromyalgia can be challenging, but many people find ways to manage their symptoms effectively. It is important to pace yourself, avoid overexertion, and build a support network of family, friends, and healthcare professionals. Joining a fibromyalgia support group can also be helpful, as it provides an opportunity to connect with others who understand what you are going through.

Learning to listen to your body and rest when needed is important, but so is staying as active as possible. Regular, gentle exercise is one of the most effective ways to reduce pain and fatigue over time.

/library/amitriptyline.bodyHtml:
What is Amitriptyline?

Amitriptyline is a type of medicine known as a tricyclic antidepressant. While it was originally developed to treat depression, it is now widely used at lower doses to help manage chronic pain conditions such as fibromyalgia, nerve pain (neuropathy), and migraines. It is also used to help with sleep problems associated with pain conditions.

How Does it Work?

Amitriptyline works by affecting the levels of certain chemicals in the brain — particularly serotonin and noradrenaline. These chemicals play a role in regulating mood, pain signals, and sleep. By increasing the availability of these chemicals, amitriptyline can reduce pain sensitivity, improve sleep quality, and lift mood.

When used for pain, amitriptyline is usually prescribed at much lower doses than when it is used for depression. Even at these lower doses, it can be very effective at reducing chronic pain and improving sleep.

Common Uses

  • Fibromyalgia
  • Nerve pain (neuropathic pain)
  • Chronic headaches and migraines
  • Depression and anxiety
  • Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)
  • Sleep disorders related to chronic pain
  • Interstitial cystitis (bladder pain)

How to Take It

Amitriptyline is taken as a tablet, usually once a day, typically in the evening. This is because it can cause drowsiness, which can actually be beneficial for those struggling with sleep. Your doctor will usually start you on a low dose and gradually increase it to find the dose that works best for you.

It is important to take amitriptyline exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Do not stop taking it suddenly without speaking to your doctor first, as this can cause withdrawal symptoms.

Side Effects

Like all medicines, amitriptyline can cause side effects, although not everyone experiences them. Common side effects include:

Most side effects are mild and tend to improve as your body gets used to the medication. If side effects are troublesome, speak to your doctor — they may be able to adjust your dose or suggest alternatives.

  • Drowsiness and dizziness (especially when first starting the medication)
  • Dry mouth
  • Constipation
  • Blurred vision
  • Weight gain
  • Difficulty urinating
  • Low blood pressure when standing up (postural hypotension)

Who Should Not Take Amitriptyline?

Amitriptyline is not suitable for everyone. It should be used with caution in people with heart conditions, epilepsy, glaucoma, or urinary problems. It is also not recommended for people who have recently had a heart attack. Always tell your doctor about all other medications you are taking, as amitriptyline can interact with many other drugs.

Important Precautions

If you are taking amitriptyline, avoid drinking alcohol as it can increase the sedative effects of the medication. Be careful when driving or operating machinery until you know how the medication affects you. If you are pregnant or breastfeeding, speak to your doctor before taking amitriptyline.

/library/naproxen.bodyHtml:
What is Naproxen?

Naproxen is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID). It is used to relieve pain, reduce inflammation (swelling), and lower fever. Naproxen is commonly used for conditions such as arthritis, gout, menstrual pain, muscle aches, headaches, and back pain. It is available on prescription and also over-the-counter (in lower doses) at pharmacies.

How Does it Work?

Naproxen works by blocking the production of prostaglandins — chemicals in the body that trigger pain, inflammation, and fever. By reducing prostaglandin production, naproxen reduces pain and swelling at the site of injury or inflammation.

Common Uses

  • Osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis
  • Gout attacks
  • Muscle and joint pain
  • Back pain
  • Menstrual (period) pain
  • Headaches and migraines
  • Ankylosing spondylitis
  • Tendonitis and bursitis

How to Take It

Naproxen is taken as a tablet or liquid. It should always be taken with or after food to reduce the risk of stomach problems. The standard adult dose is 250mg to 500mg twice daily. Always follow your doctor's or pharmacist's instructions on dosage.

Do not take naproxen for longer than directed without medical advice, as long-term use can increase the risk of serious side effects.

Side Effects

  • Stomach upset, indigestion, or heartburn
  • Nausea
  • Headache
  • Dizziness
  • Drowsiness
  • Skin rash
  • In rare cases, stomach ulcers or bleeding

Who Should Avoid Naproxen?

Naproxen is not suitable for everyone. People with stomach ulcers, kidney or liver problems, heart disease, or high blood pressure should use naproxen with caution or avoid it altogether. It is also not recommended during pregnancy, especially in the third trimester. Children under 16 should not take naproxen unless prescribed by a doctor.

Naproxen vs Ibuprofen

Both naproxen and ibuprofen are NSAIDs and work in a similar way. However, naproxen lasts longer in the body, so it is taken less frequently. Ibuprofen is generally considered milder and is more commonly available over the counter. Your doctor will advise which is more appropriate for your condition.

/library/plantar-fasciitis.bodyHtml:
What is Plantar Fasciitis?

Plantar fasciitis is one of the most common causes of heel pain. It involves inflammation of a thick band of tissue — the plantar fascia — that runs across the bottom of your foot, connecting your heel bone to your toes. The condition causes sharp, stabbing pain that is usually worst with the first few steps in the morning or after sitting for a long time.

Causes and Risk Factors

Plantar fasciitis is caused by excessive strain or repetitive stress on the plantar fascia, leading to small tears and inflammation. Risk factors include:

  • Being overweight — extra weight puts more stress on the plantar fascia
  • Occupation — jobs that involve standing for long periods on hard floors
  • Certain types of exercise — running, dancing, and other high-impact activities
  • Foot mechanics — having flat feet, a high arch, or an abnormal walking pattern
  • Age — the condition is most common between 40 and 60
  • Wearing shoes with poor arch support or thin soles

Symptoms

The hallmark symptom is a stabbing pain near the heel, usually on the bottom of the foot. This pain is typically worst after long periods of rest (such as first thing in the morning) and may improve with activity, but often returns after prolonged standing or exercise. Some people also experience:

  • Stiffness in the heel and arch
  • Swelling around the heel
  • Pain that is worse after (not during) exercise

Treatment

Most cases of plantar fasciitis improve with conservative treatments over several months:

  • Rest — reduce or modify activities that cause pain
  • Ice — apply ice to the affected area for 15–20 minutes several times daily
  • Stretching exercises — calf stretches and plantar fascia stretches
  • Supportive footwear — shoes with good arch support and cushioning
  • Orthotics — shoe inserts to distribute pressure more evenly
  • Pain relief — NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or naproxen
  • Physiotherapy
  • Night splints
  • Corticosteroid injections — for persistent cases

Recovery

With proper treatment, most people recover fully from plantar fasciitis, although it can take several months. Surgery is rarely needed and is only considered when other treatments have failed. Maintaining a healthy weight, wearing supportive shoes, and doing regular stretching exercises can help prevent recurrence.

/library/lupus.bodyHtml:
What is Lupus?

Lupus (systemic lupus erythematosus, or SLE) is a chronic autoimmune disease in which the body's immune system, which normally protects against infection, mistakenly attacks healthy tissue. This can cause inflammation and damage in many different parts of the body, including the skin, joints, kidneys, heart, lungs, and brain.

Lupus is a complex and unpredictable condition, with periods of flares (when symptoms worsen) and remissions (when symptoms improve or disappear). It affects women far more than men — about 9 out of 10 cases are in women — and tends to develop during the childbearing years (ages 15–45).

What Causes Lupus?

The exact cause of lupus is unknown, but it is thought to result from a combination of genetic, hormonal, and environmental factors. People with certain gene variants may be more likely to develop lupus, particularly when triggered by something in their environment such as sunlight, infections, or medications.

Common Symptoms

  • A butterfly-shaped rash across the cheeks and nose (malar rash)
  • Extreme fatigue
  • Joint pain, stiffness, and swelling
  • Sensitivity to sunlight (photosensitivity)
  • Skin rashes
  • Fever
  • Hair loss
  • Mouth ulcers
  • Chest pain when breathing deeply
  • Kidney problems
  • Depression and anxiety

Diagnosis

Diagnosing lupus can be challenging because its symptoms mimic many other conditions. Doctors use a combination of physical examination, blood tests, urine tests, and sometimes biopsies to reach a diagnosis. There is no single test that can definitively diagnose lupus.

Treatment

Lupus cannot be cured, but treatment can help control symptoms and prevent flares. Treatment may include:

  • Hydroxychloroquine — an antimalarial drug that reduces inflammation
  • NSAIDs — for joint pain and fever
  • Corticosteroids — to control severe inflammation
  • Immunosuppressants — for severe or organ-threatening disease
  • Lifestyle measures — avoiding sun exposure, getting adequate rest, and managing stress

Living with Lupus

Living with lupus requires ongoing management and regular medical monitoring. People with lupus should have regular check-ups to monitor organ function, especially kidney health. Sun protection is essential — wearing high-SPF sunscreen and protective clothing can help prevent flares. Many people with lupus lead full and active lives with the right support and treatment.

Who gets lupus in the UK

SLE is much more common in women than men and often starts between the mid-teens and mid-forties. It is also more common, and sometimes more severe, in people of African, Caribbean and South Asian heritage. That matters in UK clinics because delayed diagnosis is still reported when joint pain is put down to "young person's aches" or a facial rash is treated as acne or allergy. Lupus UK and NHS rheumatology teams both stress that early hydroxychloroquine and sun protection change the long-term outlook.

How UK rheumatology usually treats SLE

Almost everyone with SLE is offered hydroxychloroquine unless it is contraindicated. Flares may need a short steroid course. Organ involvement — kidneys, blood, lungs, brain — leads to immunosuppressants such as mycophenolate, azathioprine or methotrexate, and selected people are offered biologics such as belimumab. Treatment is not one-size-fits-all: a skin-and-joint picture is managed differently from lupus nephritis. Regular blood and urine tests are part of staying well, not a sign that something has already gone wrong.

/library/carpal-tunnel.bodyHtml:
What is Carpal Tunnel Syndrome?

Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) is a condition that causes numbness, tingling, and sometimes pain in the hand and fingers. It is caused by compression of the median nerve as it passes through the carpal tunnel — a narrow passageway in the wrist. CTS is one of the most common nerve disorders, affecting millions of people.

Causes and Risk Factors

  • Repetitive hand and wrist movements (e.g. typing, using a mouse)
  • Pregnancy (due to fluid retention)
  • Obesity
  • Diabetes
  • Underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism)
  • Rheumatoid arthritis
  • Wrist injuries or fractures
  • Family history of CTS

Symptoms

  • Numbness, tingling, or "pins and needles" in the thumb, index, middle, and ring fingers
  • Pain in the hand and wrist, sometimes extending up the arm
  • Weakness in the hand — difficulty gripping objects
  • Symptoms often worse at night or after prolonged hand use
  • Dropping things

Treatment

Treatment depends on the severity of symptoms. Mild to moderate cases often improve with conservative measures:

For severe or persistent cases, carpal tunnel release surgery is highly effective. This involves cutting the ligament pressing on the median nerve to relieve pressure.

  • Wrist splints — worn especially at night to keep the wrist in a neutral position
  • Corticosteroid injections — to reduce inflammation
  • Physiotherapy exercises
  • Avoiding activities that worsen symptoms
  • Treating underlying conditions (e.g. managing diabetes)

What it feels like day to day

Carpal tunnel syndrome usually creeps in. Many people first notice tingling or numbness in the thumb, index and middle fingers when they wake, and find themselves shaking the hand to get the feeling back. Holding a phone, a book or a steering wheel for a while can bring it on. The little finger is usually spared, because a different nerve supplies it.

As it progresses, fine tasks such as doing up buttons, picking up coins or opening jars can become clumsy, and you may drop things. In longer-standing cases the muscle at the base of the thumb can become thinner and weaker.

Why arthritis and carpal tunnel often go together

The carpal tunnel is a tight space, so anything that takes up room inside it can squeeze the median nerve. Inflamed tendon linings in rheumatoid arthritis, bony changes in wrist osteoarthritis, fluid retention in pregnancy, and conditions such as diabetes and an underactive thyroid can all play a part. If you have inflammatory arthritis and new carpal tunnel symptoms, tell your rheumatology team, because it can be a sign of active inflammation at the wrist.

How it is diagnosed

Your GP or physiotherapist will usually diagnose carpal tunnel syndrome from your symptoms and a hand examination, which may include simple tests that press on or stretch the nerve. If the diagnosis is unclear, symptoms are severe, or surgery is being considered, you may be referred for nerve conduction studies, which measure how well signals travel along the nerve. Blood tests can check for linked conditions such as diabetes or thyroid problems.

Things you can try first

Mild to moderate symptoms often improve without surgery, especially when started early.

  • A wrist splint worn at night keeps the wrist straight and takes pressure off the nerve. Many pharmacies sell them, and physiotherapists can advise on fit.
  • Notice what brings symptoms on. Take breaks from gripping or repetitive tasks, and keep your wrist in a neutral position when typing or using tools.
  • Try gentle nerve and tendon gliding exercises taught by a physiotherapist or hand therapist.
  • Avoid sleeping with your wrists tightly curled under your pillow or body.
  • Managing linked conditions, such as keeping diabetes or thyroid problems well controlled, can help.

Steroid injections and surgery

If splints and activity changes are not enough, a steroid injection into the carpal tunnel can reduce swelling and ease symptoms. For some people the relief is lasting, for others it wears off.

Carpal tunnel release surgery cuts the ligament that forms the roof of the tunnel, giving the nerve more room. It is usually done as a day case under local anaesthetic. Surgery is generally considered when symptoms are severe, keep coming back, or there are signs of lasting nerve damage such as constant numbness or muscle wasting. Recovery involves keeping the hand elevated and moving your fingers early, with a gradual return to heavier gripping over the following weeks.

When to get help quickly

Book a GP or physiotherapy appointment if symptoms are stopping you sleeping, are there most of the time, or you notice weakness or wasting at the base of your thumb. Seek urgent medical help if numbness or weakness comes on suddenly, affects your face, arm or leg as well as your hand, or follows a significant wrist injury, as these need checking straight away.

About this page

Written by Louis Maxwell, First Contact Practitioner (HCPC PH128483), and pending clinical review. This is general information, not a diagnosis. Always follow the advice of your own GP, physiotherapist or rheumatology team. For emergencies call 999; for urgent advice use NHS 111.

faqs.q: Will carpal tunnel syndrome go away on its own?
faqs.a: Sometimes, particularly when it is linked to pregnancy or a short spell of heavy hand use. Many people improve with a night splint and activity changes. If symptoms persist or worsen, speak to your GP or physiotherapist.

faqs.q: How long should I wear a wrist splint?
faqs.a: Night splints are usually worn every night for several weeks to see if they help. A physiotherapist or GP can advise how long to continue and whether daytime use makes sense for you.

faqs.q: Is carpal tunnel the same as arthritis?
faqs.a: No. Carpal tunnel syndrome is a squeezed nerve, while arthritis affects the joints. They can happen together, and arthritis in or around the wrist can make carpal tunnel more likely.

faqs.q: Can I self-refer to a physiotherapist for carpal tunnel?
faqs.a: In many parts of the UK you can refer yourself to NHS physiotherapy or musculoskeletal services. Check your local NHS website or ask at your GP practice.

faqs.q: How soon can I use my hand after carpal tunnel surgery?
faqs.a: Light use such as eating and dressing usually starts within days, while heavier gripping and lifting return gradually over several weeks. Your surgical team will give you a plan that fits your job and hobbies.

/library/collagen.bodyHtml:
What is Collagen?

Collagen is the most abundant protein in the human body, making up about 30% of all protein. It is the main structural component of connective tissues — including skin, tendons, ligaments, cartilage, and bones. Think of collagen as the "glue" that holds the body together, providing structure, strength, and elasticity to tissues.

Types of Collagen

There are at least 28 different types of collagen, but the most common are:

  • Type I — found in skin, tendons, bones, and ligaments (the most abundant)
  • Type II — found in cartilage, important for joint health
  • Type III — found in skin and blood vessels
  • Type IV — found in the basement membrane of organs

Why Collagen Matters for Health

Collagen plays a vital role in keeping skin plump and youthful, joints flexible and pain-free, bones strong, and gut lining intact. As we age, the body produces less collagen — production begins to decline in our mid-20s, and by our 40s and 50s, the reduction becomes more noticeable. This contributes to wrinkles, joint stiffness, and weaker bones.

Collagen Supplements

Collagen supplements (typically in the form of hydrolysed collagen or collagen peptides) have become very popular. Research suggests that supplementing with collagen may:

Collagen supplements are generally considered safe. They are available as powders, capsules, and liquids. Marine (fish-derived) and bovine (cow-derived) collagen are the most common sources.

  • Improve skin hydration and elasticity
  • Reduce joint pain — particularly in osteoarthritis
  • Support bone density
  • Help with muscle recovery after exercise

Foods That Support Collagen Production

  • Bone broth (a natural source of collagen)
  • Chicken and fish (especially the skin)
  • Eggs
  • Vitamin C-rich foods (citrus, berries, peppers) — essential for collagen synthesis
  • Zinc-rich foods (pumpkin seeds, nuts, meat)

/library/ibuprofen.bodyHtml:
What is Ibuprofen?

Ibuprofen is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID). It is one of the most commonly used over-the-counter medications in the world, used to relieve mild to moderate pain, reduce inflammation, and lower fever. It is available in tablets, capsules, gels, and liquid form.

How Does it Work?

Like other NSAIDs, ibuprofen works by blocking enzymes (COX-1 and COX-2) that produce prostaglandins — chemicals responsible for pain, inflammation, and fever. By reducing prostaglandin levels, ibuprofen effectively eases pain and reduces swelling.

What is it Used For?

  • Headaches and migraines
  • Dental pain
  • Back pain and muscle aches
  • Period pain
  • Cold and flu symptoms
  • Joint pain from arthritis
  • Sprains and strains
  • Fever in adults and children (specific children's formulations)

Dosage and How to Take it

Always take ibuprofen with or after food to protect the stomach. The usual adult dose is 200–400mg up to three times a day. Do not exceed 1,200mg in 24 hours unless directed by a doctor. Do not take for more than 10 days for pain, or 3 days for fever, without medical advice.

Side Effects

  • Stomach pain, nausea, or indigestion
  • Heartburn
  • Headache
  • Dizziness
  • Raised blood pressure with prolonged use
  • In rare cases: stomach ulcers, kidney problems, or allergic reactions

Who Should Avoid Ibuprofen?

Ibuprofen is not suitable for everyone. Avoid it if you have stomach ulcers, kidney disease, heart failure, or if you are in the third trimester of pregnancy. Children under 3 months should not be given ibuprofen. People with asthma should check with their doctor, as ibuprofen can trigger asthma attacks in some individuals.

What is Osteoarthritis?

Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common form of arthritis and a leading cause of pain and disability worldwide. It is a degenerative joint disease in which the protective cartilage that cushions the ends of bones gradually wears down over time. As the cartilage deteriorates, bones can begin to rub against each other, causing pain, stiffness, and swelling.

OA can affect any joint in the body, but it most commonly affects the knees, hips, hands, and spine. It becomes more common with age, but it is not simply an inevitable part of ageing — lifestyle factors, genetics, and previous injuries all play a role.

Causes and Risk Factors

  • Age — risk increases significantly after 50
  • Sex — women are more likely to develop OA, especially after menopause
  • Obesity — excess weight puts additional stress on weight-bearing joints
  • Previous joint injuries
  • Repetitive movements from work or sport
  • Family history of OA
  • Joint deformities or abnormalities

Symptoms

  • Joint pain, especially after activity or at the end of the day
  • Stiffness — particularly in the morning or after sitting
  • Swelling around the affected joint
  • A grating or crackling sensation (crepitus) when moving the joint
  • Reduced range of movement
  • Bony growths (osteophytes) around the joint

Treatment

There is no cure for OA, but treatments can effectively manage symptoms:

  • Exercise — low-impact activities like swimming, cycling, and walking strengthen muscles around the joint
  • Weight management — losing weight reduces pressure on joints
  • Pain relief — paracetamol, NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen)
  • Physiotherapy
  • Corticosteroid injections
  • Assistive devices — walking sticks, knee braces
  • Joint replacement surgery — for severe cases

What is Rheumatoid Arthritis?

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks the lining of joints (the synovium), causing inflammation, pain, swelling, and eventually joint damage. Unlike osteoarthritis, which results from wear and tear, RA is an inflammatory condition driven by the immune system. It can affect people of all ages, including children, but most commonly develops between the ages of 40 and 60. Women are two to three times more likely to develop RA than men.

What Causes it?

The exact cause of RA is unknown, but it involves a combination of genetic susceptibility and environmental triggers. Smoking is the strongest known environmental risk factor. Other possible triggers include infections, hormonal changes, and physical or emotional stress.

Symptoms

  • Joint pain, swelling, and tenderness — especially in the small joints of the hands and feet
  • Morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes
  • Symmetrical joint involvement (both sides of the body affected)
  • Fatigue and general feeling of being unwell
  • Low-grade fever
  • Rheumatoid nodules (firm bumps under the skin)
  • In severe cases, complications affecting the eyes, heart, and lungs

Diagnosis

Diagnosis involves blood tests (including for rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies), imaging (X-rays, ultrasound, MRI), and a physical examination. Early diagnosis is crucial as prompt treatment can prevent joint damage.

Treatment

RA is treated with disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs), which slow disease progression and prevent joint damage. Methotrexate is usually the first DMARD prescribed. Biologics (such as adalimumab) are used for moderate to severe RA that does not respond to conventional DMARDs. NSAIDs and corticosteroids are used to manage inflammation and pain.

/library/arthritis.bodyHtml:
What is Arthritis?

Arthritis is not a single disease — it is an umbrella term for more than 100 different conditions that cause pain, inflammation, and stiffness in the joints. The word "arthritis" comes from the Greek words for joint (arthron) and inflammation (itis). It is one of the most common chronic conditions in the UK, affecting over 10 million people.

Types of Arthritis

The two most common types are osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis, but there are many others, including:

  • Psoriatic arthritis — linked to the skin condition psoriasis
  • Gout — caused by uric acid crystal build-up in joints
  • Ankylosing spondylitis — affects the spine
  • Reactive arthritis — triggered by an infection elsewhere in the body
  • Lupus arthritis
  • Juvenile idiopathic arthritis — affects children

Common Symptoms

  • Joint pain and tenderness
  • Stiffness — especially in the morning
  • Swelling and warmth around joints
  • Reduced range of movement
  • Redness over the joint
  • Fatigue

Managing Arthritis

Treatment depends on the type of arthritis. General strategies include regular low-impact exercise, maintaining a healthy weight, taking prescribed medications, physiotherapy, and in severe cases, surgery. Many people with arthritis also benefit from occupational therapy to help adapt daily activities and reduce strain on joints.

Can Arthritis Be Prevented?

Not all types of arthritis can be prevented, but you can reduce your risk by maintaining a healthy weight, staying active, protecting joints from injury, not smoking, and eating a balanced diet rich in anti-inflammatory foods.

/library/lupus-symptoms.answer: Lupus (SLE) is well known for causing a wide and varied range of symptoms that can come and go unpredictably. /library/lupus-symptoms.bodyHtml:
Overview

Lupus (SLE) is well known for causing a wide and varied range of symptoms that can come and go unpredictably. Because symptoms can mimic so many other conditions, lupus is often called the "great imitator." No two people with lupus experience exactly the same symptoms, and they can range from mild to life-threatening.

The Butterfly Rash

One of the most recognisable signs of lupus is a butterfly-shaped rash (malar rash) that spreads across both cheeks and the bridge of the nose. This rash may be flat or slightly raised and is typically red or purple. It can be triggered or worsened by sun exposure and tends to come and go with disease activity.

Fatigue

Extreme fatigue is one of the most common and debilitating symptoms of lupus. Unlike normal tiredness, lupus fatigue can be overwhelming and not relieved by sleep or rest. It can significantly impact daily activities, work, and quality of life.

Joint and Muscle Symptoms

  • Pain, stiffness, and swelling in multiple joints
  • Muscle aches and weakness
  • Morning stiffness

Skin and Hair

  • Photosensitivity — skin rashes triggered by sunlight
  • Discoid rash — a thick, scaly rash on the face, scalp, or neck
  • Hair loss (alopecia)
  • Raynaud's phenomenon — fingers and toes turn white or blue in the cold

Kidney Involvement (Lupus Nephritis)

Lupus can damage the kidneys, causing a condition called lupus nephritis. Signs include foamy or bloody urine, high blood pressure, and swelling in the legs. Regular urine and blood tests are essential to monitor kidney function.

Other Symptoms

  • Mouth or nose ulcers
  • Chest pain when breathing deeply (pleuritis or pericarditis)
  • Dry eyes
  • Seizures or neurological problems
  • Depression and cognitive difficulties

How this library note differs from the condition hub

The condition hub at /conditions/lupus/symptoms is a structured checklist for people already thinking in NHS pathway terms. This library note is the slower explainer: why the same person can look well one week and exhausted the next, how a malar rash differs from rosacea or sunburn, and which combinations of symptoms should prompt a GP appointment rather than another month of waiting. It is written for first searches such as "lupus symptoms UK" and "butterfly rash and joint pain".

Early signs people in the UK often miss

Lupus is called the great imitator because early features look like viral illness, stress, or "just being run down". Many people see their GP several times before anyone mentions SLE. Patterns that deserve a second look include fatigue that is not explained by a normal blood count, joint pain that moves between the hands and knees without lasting damage, mouth ulcers that keep returning, and a facial rash that flares after a bright UK day even when it is not hot.

  • Unexplained fevers or night sweats alongside joint aches
  • Hair thinning at the temples or a sore scalp after sun
  • Fingers that blanch white then blue in the cold (Raynaud's)
  • Chest pain that is worse when you breathe in (pleurisy)
  • Puffy ankles, foamy urine or rising blood pressure — possible kidney involvement

Butterfly rash versus other facial rashes

The classic malar rash sits across both cheeks and the bridge of the nose and usually spares the nasolabial folds (the creases from nose to mouth). It may be flat or slightly raised, pink to purple, and often worsens after UV exposure. Rosacea tends to spare the same folds less reliably and comes with flushing and visible vessels. Eczema itches and often has a personal or family history of atopy. If a rash appears with joint pain, mouth ulcers or extreme fatigue, mention lupus specifically — GPs see facial rashes every day and will not automatically think of SLE.

Fatigue, flares and working or studying

Lupus fatigue is not ordinary tiredness. People describe a flu-like heaviness that sleep does not lift. Flares can be triggered by UV light, infection, some medicines, and poorly managed stress. In the UK, occupational health, Access to Work and reasonable adjustments under the Equality Act 2010 are relevant if fatigue or photosensitivity affects a job or course. A short symptom diary — energy, rash, joint swelling, urine changes — helps a rheumatology nurse see the pattern between six-monthly appointments.

Tests your GP can start before rheumatology

There is no single lupus test. A GP can request a full blood count, kidney and liver function, urine dip and protein, ESR or CRP, and an antinuclear antibody (ANA) screen. A positive ANA is common and does not mean you have lupus on its own; a negative ANA makes SLE less likely. If clinical suspicion is high, ask about anti-dsDNA, ENA, complement (C3 and C4) and antiphospholipid antibodies. NICE-aligned practice is to refer to rheumatology when inflammatory symptoms persist and bloods or urine suggest a systemic disease.

When lupus symptoms are urgent

Most lupus symptoms can wait for a GP appointment. Seek same-day or emergency care if you have severe chest pain or breathlessness, a sudden severe headache with confusion, markedly reduced urine output with swelling, a high fever while on immunosuppressants, or new weakness or seizure. These can signal organ-threatening disease or infection — both need urgent assessment, not another library search.

/library/osteoporosis.question: Osteoporosis
/library/osteoporosis.answer: Osteoporosis is a condition in which bones become weak and brittle — so brittle that a fall or even mild stresses such as bending over or coughing can cause a fracture. The word osteoporosis means "porous bone." In someone with osteoporosis, the holes and spaces inside the bone are much larger than in healthy bone.
/library/osteoporosis.bodyHtml:
What is Osteoporosis?

Osteoporosis is a condition in which bones become weak and brittle — so brittle that a fall or even mild stresses such as bending over or coughing can cause a fracture. The word osteoporosis means "porous bone." In someone with osteoporosis, the holes and spaces inside the bone are much larger than in healthy bone.

Osteoporosis affects over 3 million people in the UK. It is more common in women — especially after the menopause — but men can also develop it. Fractures from osteoporosis most commonly occur in the hip, wrist, and spine.

Who is at Risk?

  • Women after the menopause (oestrogen helps maintain bone density)
  • Older adults
  • People with a family history of osteoporosis or hip fractures
  • Those who smoke or drink heavily
  • People with low body weight
  • Those with conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, coeliac disease, or Crohn's disease
  • Long-term use of corticosteroid medications
  • People with low vitamin D or calcium levels

Symptoms

Osteoporosis is often called a "silent disease" because there are no symptoms until a fracture occurs. Signs that may suggest you have osteoporosis include a loss of height over time, a stooped posture, and back pain caused by fractured vertebrae.

Diagnosis

A DEXA (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry) scan is used to measure bone density and diagnose osteoporosis. A score below -2.5 indicates osteoporosis.

Treatment and Prevention

  • Calcium and vitamin D supplements
  • Bisphosphonate medications (e.g. alendronic acid) — the most commonly prescribed drugs for osteoporosis
  • Weight-bearing and resistance exercise — strengthens bones
  • Quit smoking and reduce alcohol intake
  • Fall prevention — home safety modifications, balance exercises
  • Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) — for some postmenopausal women

/library/bursitis.bodyHtml:
What is Bursitis?

Bursitis is inflammation of the bursae — small, fluid-filled sacs that cushion bones, tendons, and muscles near the joints. Bursae reduce friction and allow smooth movement between tissues. When a bursa becomes inflamed, it causes pain and swelling near the affected joint. Bursitis most commonly occurs in the shoulder, elbow, hip, and knee.

Causes

  • Repetitive movements or prolonged pressure on a joint
  • Sudden injury or trauma
  • Rheumatoid arthritis or gout
  • Infection (septic bursitis)
  • Certain occupations (e.g. carpet laying, gardening)

Symptoms

  • Aching or stiffness in the affected joint
  • Swelling and redness
  • Pain that worsens with movement or pressure
  • Limited range of motion

Treatment

Most cases of bursitis improve within a few weeks with proper rest and treatment. Avoiding the activities that caused it helps prevent recurrence.

  • Rest the affected joint
  • Apply ice for 20 minutes several times a day
  • Anti-inflammatory medications (NSAIDs)
  • Physiotherapy exercises
  • Corticosteroid injections
  • Draining the bursa (aspiration) if severely swollen
  • Antibiotics for infected bursitis

/library/raynauds.answer: Raynaud's disease (also called Raynaud's phenomenon or syndrome) is a condition that affects blood supply to certain parts of the body — usually the fingers and toes — causing them to feel numb and cold in response to cold temperatures or stress. /library/raynauds.bodyHtml:
What is Raynaud's Disease?

Raynaud's disease (also called Raynaud's phenomenon or syndrome) is a condition that affects blood supply to certain parts of the body — usually the fingers and toes — causing them to feel numb and cold in response to cold temperatures or stress. During an episode, affected areas typically turn white (due to reduced blood flow), then blue (from lack of oxygen), then red (as blood returns). Episodes usually last a few minutes but can last longer.

Types

There are two types of Raynaud's:

  • Primary Raynaud's — not linked to any other disease; the most common type, often mild
  • Secondary Raynaud's — caused by an underlying condition, such as lupus, scleroderma, or rheumatoid arthritis; tends to be more severe

Triggers

  • Cold temperatures
  • Emotional stress
  • Holding cold objects
  • Air conditioning

Management

  • Keep warm — wear gloves, warm socks, and layers
  • Avoid sudden temperature changes
  • Exercise regularly to improve circulation
  • Stop smoking
  • Manage stress
  • Medications — calcium channel blockers (e.g. nifedipine) to widen blood vessels

What happens during an attack

In Raynaud's, small blood vessels in the fingers and toes overreact to cold or stress and narrow sharply. The skin often turns white, then blue as oxygen drops, then red as blood rushes back. Fingers can feel numb, painful, tingly or throb as they warm up. Attacks can last from a few minutes to much longer. Toes, ears, nose and nipples can also be affected.

Primary and secondary Raynaud's

Primary Raynaud's happens on its own, often starting in the teens or twenties. It is usually a nuisance rather than a danger.

Secondary Raynaud's happens because of another condition, most often an autoimmune condition such as scleroderma (systemic sclerosis), lupus, Sjögren's or rheumatoid arthritis. Some medicines, smoking and heavy use of vibrating tools can also cause it. Secondary Raynaud's is more likely to start later in life, affect only some fingers, be severe, or cause skin sores.

How a GP will assess it

Your GP will ask about your attacks, other symptoms such as joint pain, rashes, tight skin, dry eyes or mouth and difficulty swallowing, and your medicines. They may arrange blood tests, including tests for autoimmune conditions. A specialist may look at the tiny blood vessels at the base of your nails with a magnifier (capillaroscopy), which helps show whether an underlying condition is likely.

Keeping warm and preventing attacks

Keeping your whole body warm matters as much as warming your hands.

  • Dress in layers and keep your core warm; wear a hat and warm socks.
  • Use gloves or mittens outdoors and when handling cold food from the fridge or freezer.
  • Try hand and foot warmers, heated gloves or insoles on cold days.
  • Warm the car before you set off, and avoid sudden moves from warm rooms into cold air where possible.
  • Stop smoking, as it narrows blood vessels further; your GP or pharmacy can help.
  • Keep active to help circulation, and find ways to manage stress, which can trigger attacks.
  • If an attack starts, move somewhere warm and warm your hands gently in lukewarm, not hot, water or under your armpits.

Medicines and specialist treatment

If self-help is not enough, your GP may suggest a medicine that relaxes blood vessels, most commonly a calcium channel blocker. Your GP will talk through side effects such as headaches, flushing or ankle swelling. Your GP will also review any current medicines that could be making Raynaud's worse. People with severe secondary Raynaud's, especially with finger ulcers, are usually cared for by a rheumatology team, who have further treatments available, including hospital-based infusions.

When to see a GP or get urgent help

See your GP if Raynaud's starts after about age 30, affects only one side or a few fingers, is very painful, or comes with joint pain, rashes, tight skin, tiredness, dry eyes or mouth, or difficulty swallowing. Seek urgent medical advice the same day if a finger or toe develops a sore or ulcer, turns black, or stays white or blue and cold rather than recovering after warming.

About this page

Written by Louis Maxwell, First Contact Practitioner (HCPC PH128483), and pending clinical review. This is general information, not a diagnosis. Always follow the advice of your own GP, physiotherapist or rheumatology team. For emergencies call 999; for urgent advice use NHS 111.

faqs.q: Is Raynaud's serious?
faqs.a: Primary Raynaud's is usually uncomfortable but not dangerous. Secondary Raynaud's can be linked to conditions that need specialist care, so new or severe symptoms should be checked by a GP.

faqs.q: Can Raynaud's be cured?
faqs.a: There is no cure, but most people can reduce how often and how badly attacks happen by keeping warm, stopping smoking and, if needed, using medicines that widen blood vessels.

faqs.q: Is Raynaud's linked to arthritis?
faqs.a: It can be. Raynaud's is common in autoimmune conditions such as scleroderma, lupus and Sjögren's, and sometimes occurs with rheumatoid arthritis.

faqs.q: What should I do during an attack?
faqs.a: Get somewhere warm, warm your whole body, and gently warm your hands or feet in lukewarm water or under your armpits. Avoid very hot water, which can hurt numb skin.

faqs.q: When is Raynaud's an emergency?
faqs.a: Seek same-day medical advice if a finger or toe develops an ulcer, turns black, or stays cold and discoloured instead of recovering after warming.

/library/ankylosing-spondylitis.bodyHtml:
What is Ankylosing Spondylitis?

Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a type of inflammatory arthritis that primarily affects the spine and the sacroiliac joints (where the spine meets the pelvis). Over time, inflammation can cause the vertebrae in the spine to fuse together, leading to a rigid, inflexible spine — a process called ankylosis. AS is part of a broader group of conditions called spondyloarthropathies.

AS most commonly develops in teenagers and young adults in their 20s and 30s. It is more common in men than women, though women tend to experience milder symptoms. There is a strong genetic association — most people with AS carry the HLA-B27 gene.

Symptoms

  • Chronic lower back pain and stiffness — especially in the morning
  • Symptoms improve with exercise and worsen with rest
  • Neck pain and stiffness
  • Fatigue
  • Inflammation in other joints (hips, shoulders, knees)
  • Enthesitis — pain and tenderness where tendons and ligaments attach to bone
  • Eye inflammation (uveitis) — causing red, painful eyes
  • Difficulty breathing deeply (in advanced cases, if the rib cage is affected)

Treatment

  • NSAIDs — the first-line treatment for pain and stiffness
  • Physiotherapy and regular exercise — essential for maintaining flexibility
  • Biologics — TNF inhibitors or IL-17 inhibitors for moderate to severe AS
  • Posture training and hydrotherapy

Why GPs still miss inflammatory back pain

Most back pain in UK primary care is mechanical. AS (now often called axial spondyloarthritis) is the exception that improves with movement and worsens with rest. Pain that wakes you in the second half of the night, stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes, buttock pain that swaps sides, and a start before age 45 are the clues NICE NG65 asks clinicians to look for. People often spend years being told to 'keep stretching' without an HLA-B27 test, CRP, or rheumatology referral.

More than the spine

AS can inflame the eyes (uveitis — a red, painful, light-sensitive eye that needs same-day ophthalmology), the heels and Achilles insertions, and sometimes the gut or skin. Chest wall involvement makes a deep breath feel tight. These extra-spinal features are why a 'bad back' story plus a red eye should not be treated as two unrelated problems.

What good UK care looks like

NASS and rheumatology teams treat daily spinal mobility work as medicine, not an optional extra. NSAIDs are often taken regularly rather than as required. If inflammation stays active, NHS pathways include TNF or IL-17 inhibitors. Physiotherapy, hydrotherapy and a smoking-cessation conversation (smoking worsens AS) sit alongside drugs. This library page is the overview; the condition subpages cover treatment, diet and exercises in more depth.

/library/gout-symptoms.bodyHtml:
What is Gout?

Gout is a type of inflammatory arthritis caused by high levels of uric acid in the blood. When uric acid builds up, it can form sharp crystals in a joint, causing sudden and severe pain. Gout attacks often strike without warning and are notoriously painful — many sufferers describe them as one of the most intense pains they have ever felt.

Key Symptoms of a Gout Attack

  • Intense joint pain — most commonly in the big toe, but also ankle, knee, wrist, and elbow
  • The joint is hot, red, and very tender — even the weight of a bed sheet can be unbearable
  • Swelling and inflammation around the joint
  • Attacks typically begin suddenly, often at night
  • Symptoms peak within 12–24 hours
  • Lingering discomfort after the acute pain subsides

What Triggers Gout?

  • Eating purine-rich foods (red meat, organ meats, shellfish)
  • Drinking alcohol — especially beer and spirits
  • Sugary drinks containing fructose
  • Dehydration
  • Certain medications (diuretics, low-dose aspirin)
  • Illness, surgery, or physical trauma

Managing Gout Symptoms

  • Rest the affected joint and elevate it
  • Apply ice to reduce swelling
  • NSAIDs (naproxen, ibuprofen) for pain relief
  • Colchicine — highly effective for acute gout attacks
  • Corticosteroids if NSAIDs are not suitable
  • Allopurinol — for long-term prevention by lowering uric acid levels
  • Stay well hydrated
  • Dietary changes to reduce uric acid

What a first UK attack usually looks like

A first gout attack often wakes someone in the small hours with a red-hot big toe that cannot bear a bedsheet. The joint looks shiny, and walking to the bathroom is miserable. Ankles, knees, wrists and elbows can be hit instead. Attacks typically peak within a day and settle over one to two weeks. Between attacks the joint can look completely normal — which is why people delay seeing a GP until the third or fourth episode.

Symptoms that are not gout

An infected joint (septic arthritis) is a medical emergency: severe pain, fever and inability to move the joint need same-day urgent care, not a wait-and-see gout plan. Cellulitis around the foot can also look red and hot. If this is your first attack, ask for a diagnosis rather than assuming it is gout from a photograph. Joint fluid analysis is the gold standard when the picture is unclear.

After the pain: what your GP should discuss

UK guidance treats gout as a long-term urate problem, not a series of bad nights. After even one confirmed attack, many people benefit from a conversation about urate-lowering treatment (usually allopurinol), a target blood urate, and lifestyle steps that help but do not replace medicine. Recurring attacks, tophi, kidney stones or CKD make long-term treatment more important, not less.

/library/methotrexate.answer: Methotrexate is a disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) used to treat a range of inflammatory and autoimmune conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, and psoriasis. It works by suppressing the overactive immune response that causes inflammation and joint damage in these conditions. Methot
/library/methotrexate.bodyHtml:
What is Methotrexate?

Methotrexate is a disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) used to treat a range of inflammatory and autoimmune conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, and psoriasis. It works by suppressing the overactive immune response that causes inflammation and joint damage in these conditions. Methotrexate is also used in cancer treatment at much higher doses.

How Does it Work for Arthritis?

In autoimmune conditions, methotrexate interferes with the production of cells involved in inflammation. It helps reduce joint inflammation, prevent joint damage, and improve physical function. It does not provide immediate pain relief — it typically takes 6–12 weeks to notice significant benefit.

How is it Taken?

For arthritis, methotrexate is usually taken once a week — this is crucial to remember, as taking it every day would be dangerous. It can be taken as a tablet or by injection. Folic acid (usually 5mg once a week, on a different day to methotrexate) is prescribed alongside it to reduce side effects.

Side Effects

  • Nausea and stomach upset (often on the day of or after taking it)
  • Mouth sores
  • Fatigue
  • Liver problems — regular blood tests to monitor liver function are required
  • Lowered immunity — increased risk of infections
  • Rare: lung problems (methotrexate pneumonitis)

Important Precautions

Methotrexate must not be taken during pregnancy or when trying to conceive (men and women). Regular blood tests are essential to monitor liver, kidney, and blood cell counts. Alcohol should be avoided or minimised. Vaccinations should be discussed with your doctor before taking live vaccines.

/library/turmeric.bodyHtml:
What is Turmeric?

Turmeric is a bright yellow spice derived from the root of the Curcuma longa plant, native to South Asia. It has been used for thousands of years in cooking, traditional Ayurvedic medicine, and as a natural dye. In recent decades, turmeric — and specifically its active compound curcumin — has attracted significant scientific interest for its potential health benefits.

Curcumin: The Active Ingredient

Curcumin is the main bioactive compound in turmeric and is responsible for most of its health-promoting properties. Curcumin is a powerful anti-inflammatory and antioxidant. However, curcumin makes up only about 3% of turmeric by weight, and it is poorly absorbed by the body on its own. Taking curcumin with black pepper (which contains piperine) can increase absorption by up to 2,000%.

Potential Health Benefits

  • Anti-inflammatory — may help reduce inflammation in conditions like arthritis, IBD, and other chronic diseases
  • Antioxidant — neutralises free radicals that damage cells
  • Joint health — some studies suggest curcumin may reduce joint pain and stiffness in osteoarthritis
  • Digestive health — traditional use as a digestive aid
  • Brain health — may support cognitive function and help protect against age-related decline
  • Heart health — may improve heart disease risk factors

How to Use Turmeric

  • Add to curries, soups, and stews
  • Make "golden milk" — turmeric mixed with warm milk and black pepper
  • Take as a supplement (curcumin extract with piperine)

Is it Safe?

Turmeric is generally considered safe when consumed as a food. High doses of curcumin supplements may cause stomach upset and can interact with blood-thinning medications. Speak to your doctor before taking turmeric supplements if you are on any medication.

What is Acupuncture?

Acupuncture is a traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) practice that involves inserting very fine needles into specific points on the body to stimulate the flow of energy (known as "qi" or "chi"). According to traditional Chinese medicine, illness occurs when the flow of qi is blocked or disrupted. Modern Western medicine explains acupuncture's effects in terms of stimulating nerves, muscles, and connective tissue, which may boost the body's natural painkillers and promote healing.

What Can it Help?

The evidence for acupuncture varies depending on the condition. the UK healthcare system and NICE (National Institute for Health and Care Excellence) recommends acupuncture for certain types of chronic pain, including:

Other conditions for which acupuncture is commonly used, though evidence is less established, include fibromyalgia, menstrual pain, nausea, anxiety, and insomnia.

  • Chronic primary pain
  • Tension-type headaches
  • Migraines
  • Low back pain
  • Neck pain
  • Osteoarthritis

What to Expect from a Session

A typical acupuncture session lasts between 30 and 60 minutes. The practitioner will assess your health and insert needles at appropriate points. The needles are left in place for up to 30 minutes. Most people feel very little discomfort — a mild tingling or dull ache is common. A course of treatment usually involves several sessions.

Is it Safe?

Acupuncture is generally very safe when performed by a trained and qualified practitioner. Side effects are rare but can include slight bruising, bleeding, or dizziness. Make sure your acupuncturist is registered with a recognised professional body such as the British Acupuncture Council.

/library/allopurinol.title: Allopurinol | Living With Arthritis UK
/library/allopurinol.description: Long-term treatment to prevent gout attacks
/library/allopurinol.question: Allopurinol
/library/allopurinol.answer: Allopurinol is a medication used to lower uric acid levels in the blood. It is the most commonly prescribed long-term treatment for gout. High levels of uric acid cause the formation of crystals in the joints, which leads to painful gout attacks. By reducing uric acid production, allopurinol helps prevent these attacks
/library/allopurinol.bodyHtml:
What is Allopurinol?

Allopurinol is a medication used to lower uric acid levels in the blood. It is the most commonly prescribed long-term treatment for gout. High levels of uric acid cause the formation of crystals in the joints, which leads to painful gout attacks. By reducing uric acid production, allopurinol helps prevent these attacks and, over time, dissolves existing crystals.

Who is it For?

Allopurinol is recommended for people who:

  • Have frequent gout attacks (two or more per year)
  • Have tophaceous gout (visible uric acid crystal deposits)
  • Have gout-related kidney problems
  • Have kidney stones caused by uric acid

How to Take it

Allopurinol is taken as a daily tablet, usually starting at 100mg and gradually increasing. It must be taken long-term — it is not a cure and should not be stopped without medical advice. Importantly, allopurinol should not be started during an acute gout attack, as it can initially worsen symptoms. It should be started once the attack has fully resolved.

Side Effects

  • Rash — if you develop a rash, stop taking it and see your doctor immediately, as a rare but serious allergic reaction (Stevens-Johnson syndrome) is possible
  • Nausea and stomach upset
  • Increased frequency of gout attacks when first starting (this should settle)
  • Drowsiness

Monitoring

Regular blood tests are needed to check uric acid levels and kidney function. The target uric acid level is usually below 300–360 micromol/L. Drinking plenty of water (at least 2 litres a day) is recommended to help flush uric acid from the body.

/library/knee-pain.title: Knee pain: common causes and what you can do about it
/library/knee-pain.description: Sore knee when walking, kneeling or on stairs? Understand the common causes, self-help that works, when to rest or move, and when to see a GP or physio.
/library/knee-pain.question: Knee pain: common causes and what you can do about it
/library/knee-pain.answer: Knee pain is one of the most common complaints, affecting people of all ages. It can result from injuries, overuse, or underlying conditions such as arthritis. The knee is the largest and most complex joint in the body, making it vulnerable to a wide range of problems.
/library/knee-pain.bodyHtml:
Overview

Knee pain is one of the most common complaints, affecting people of all ages. It can result from injuries, overuse, or underlying conditions such as arthritis. The knee is the largest and most complex joint in the body, making it vulnerable to a wide range of problems.

Common Causes

  • Osteoarthritis — wear and tear of the knee joint cartilage
  • Ligament injuries — such as ACL or MCL tears
  • Meniscus tears — damage to the cartilage pads in the knee
  • Bursitis — inflammation of the fluid-filled sacs
  • Patellar tendonitis — inflammation of the tendon below the kneecap
  • IT band syndrome — from overuse in runners
  • Patellofemoral syndrome — pain around the kneecap
  • Gout — uric acid crystals in the knee joint

Symptoms

  • Pain — ranging from a dull ache to sharp, stabbing pain
  • Swelling and stiffness
  • Weakness or instability
  • Popping or crunching sounds
  • Difficulty fully straightening or bending the knee

Treatment Options

  • RICE method — Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation
  • Pain medications — paracetamol, NSAIDs
  • Physiotherapy — strengthening and stretching exercises
  • Knee supports and braces
  • Weight management
  • Corticosteroid or hyaluronic acid injections
  • Surgery for severe damage (knee replacement, arthroscopy)

Common causes by pattern

Knee pain has many causes, and where and when it hurts gives useful clues. This list is a guide, not a diagnosis.

  • Aching when walking or on stairs, stiffness after sitting, and sometimes creaking, especially over 45: often knee osteoarthritis.
  • Pain around or behind the kneecap, worse on stairs, squatting or after sitting with bent knees: often patellofemoral pain, common in active younger people.
  • Pain on the inner or outer side after a twist, sometimes with swelling, catching or locking: may be a meniscus (cartilage) problem.
  • Pain just below the kneecap in people who run or jump: often a tendon problem.
  • A soft swelling on the front of the knee after a lot of kneeling: may be bursitis.
  • Swelling of several joints, long morning stiffness or feeling unwell: may be inflammatory arthritis, which needs a GP review.
  • A sudden, very painful, hot, red swollen big toe or knee: can be gout or pseudogout.

What helps most knee pain

For most everyday knee pain, keeping moving is more helpful than prolonged rest. Rest from the activity that provokes it for a short time if you need to, but stay active in other ways.

Strengthening the muscles at the front and back of the thigh and around the hip is one of the most reliable ways to reduce knee pain and improve function, including in osteoarthritis. Start with a few simple exercises such as sit-to-stands from a chair, straight leg raises and step-ups, and build up gradually. Some discomfort during exercise is normal, but pain should settle back to your usual level within a day.

Other things that help include losing weight if you are carrying extra, comfortable shock-absorbing shoes, a walking pole or stick in the opposite hand on bad days, and anti-inflammatory gel on the knee after checking with a pharmacist.

Resting, icing and supports

After a minor strain, short-term measures such as relative rest, an ice pack wrapped in a towel and elevation can ease swelling. For stiff, arthritic knees many people prefer warmth. Knee sleeves and supports can make some people feel more confident, but they do not replace strengthening. Avoid wearing a brace all day unless a clinician has recommended it.

Seeing a professional

In many areas you can refer yourself to NHS physiotherapy or a first contact practitioner at your GP surgery. They can examine your knee, explain what is going on and set up an exercise plan. X-rays are not always needed to diagnose knee osteoarthritis in people over 45 with typical symptoms, and scans are usually reserved for when the result would change what happens next.

When to seek urgent help

Some knee problems need prompt medical attention.

  • Go to A&E or call 999 if the knee is hot, red and very swollen and you have a fever or feel unwell, because a joint infection needs same-day treatment.
  • Go to A&E or an urgent treatment centre if you cannot put weight on the leg after an injury, the knee looks deformed, or you heard a pop followed by rapid swelling.
  • Get urgent medical help if your calf is swollen, red and painful, as this can be a blood clot.
  • See your GP soon if the knee keeps locking or giving way, or if several joints are swollen.

About this page

Written by Louis Maxwell, First Contact Practitioner (HCPC PH128483), and pending clinical review. This is general information, not a diagnosis. Always follow the advice of your own GP, physiotherapist or rheumatology team. For emergencies call 999; for urgent advice use NHS 111.

faqs.q: Should I rest or exercise a painful knee?
faqs.a: For most knee pain, gentle activity and strengthening help more than prolonged rest. Ease off the activity that aggravates it for a short time, keep moving in other ways, and build up gradually.

faqs.q: Do I need an X-ray for knee pain?
faqs.a: Not always. Knee osteoarthritis can usually be diagnosed from your symptoms and an examination if you are over 45. Imaging is used when the result would change your care or when a different problem is suspected.

faqs.q: Is it safe to walk with knee arthritis?
faqs.a: Yes, walking is generally good for knee arthritis. Pace yourself, wear supportive shoes, and use a stick in the opposite hand on bad days if it helps.

faqs.q: Why does my knee hurt more going downstairs?
faqs.a: Going downstairs puts more load through the front of the knee and relies on thigh muscles working while lengthening. Strengthening exercises and using the handrail often help.

faqs.q: When is knee pain an emergency?
faqs.a: Seek urgent help if the knee is hot, red and swollen with a fever, if you cannot bear weight after an injury, or if your calf is swollen and painful.
