/library/psoriatic-arthritis.description: Arthritis linked to the skin condition psoriasis
/library/psoriatic-arthritis.question: Psoriatic Arthritis
/library/psoriatic-arthritis.answer: Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) is a type of inflammatory arthritis that affects some people who have psoriasis — a chronic skin condition causing red, scaly patches. PsA causes joint pain, stiffness, and swelling, and can affect any joint in the body. It can also affect the spine (psoriatic spondylitis), fingernails and toe
/library/psoriatic-arthritis.bodyHtml:
What is Psoriatic Arthritis?

Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) is a type of inflammatory arthritis that affects some people who have psoriasis — a chronic skin condition causing red, scaly patches. PsA causes joint pain, stiffness, and swelling, and can affect any joint in the body. It can also affect the spine (psoriatic spondylitis), fingernails and toenails (nail psoriasis), and cause a sausage-like swelling of entire fingers or toes (dactylitis).

About 20–30% of people with psoriasis develop psoriatic arthritis. It affects men and women equally and most commonly develops between the ages of 30 and 50.

Symptoms

  • Joint pain and swelling
  • Morning stiffness
  • Dactylitis — swollen, sausage-shaped fingers or toes
  • Nail changes — pitting, thickening, or separation from the nail bed
  • Enthesitis — pain at tendon and ligament attachment sites
  • Back pain and stiffness (in spinal involvement)
  • Fatigue

Treatment

  • NSAIDs — for mild symptoms
  • DMARDs — methotrexate, sulfasalazine, leflunomide
  • Biologics — TNF inhibitors (adalimumab, etanercept), IL-12/23, IL-17 inhibitors
  • JAK inhibitors — newer targeted treatments
  • Physiotherapy and exercise
  • Skin treatments for psoriasis

/library/sjogrens.title: Sjögren's: dry eyes, dry mouth and tiredness explained
/library/sjogrens.description: Sjögren's causes dry eyes, dry mouth, joint pain and fatigue. Learn how it is diagnosed, practical relief for dryness, dental care and treatment options.
/library/sjogrens.question: Sjögren's: dry eyes, dry mouth and tiredness explained
/library/sjogrens.answer: Sjögren's syndrome is a chronic autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks moisture-producing glands throughout the body — particularly the tear glands (lacrimal glands) and salivary glands. This leads to the hallmark symptoms of dry eyes and dry mouth. It can occur on its own (primary Sjögren's) or alongs
/library/sjogrens.bodyHtml:
What is Sjögren's Syndrome?

Sjögren's syndrome is a chronic autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks moisture-producing glands throughout the body — particularly the tear glands (lacrimal glands) and salivary glands. This leads to the hallmark symptoms of dry eyes and dry mouth. It can occur on its own (primary Sjögren's) or alongside other autoimmune conditions such as lupus or rheumatoid arthritis (secondary Sjögren's).

Sjögren's syndrome is more common in women (nine times more than men) and typically develops after the age of 40.

Symptoms

  • Dry eyes — gritty, burning, or itchy sensation
  • Dry mouth — difficulty swallowing or speaking
  • Fatigue — often severe
  • Joint pain and stiffness
  • Swollen salivary glands
  • Skin dryness
  • Vaginal dryness
  • Dental problems — dry mouth increases cavity risk
  • Nerve problems (peripheral neuropathy)

Treatment

There is no cure for Sjögren's, but symptoms can be managed:

  • Eye drops and gels — artificial tears for dry eyes
  • Saliva substitutes and stimulants for dry mouth
  • Hydroxychloroquine — reduces fatigue and joint pain
  • NSAIDs for joint pain
  • Immunosuppressants for severe cases
  • Good dental hygiene and regular dental check-ups

More than dry eyes and mouth

Dryness is the best-known feature of Sjögren's, but for many people the tiredness is just as hard to live with. Joint and muscle aches are common, and some people have Raynaud's, dry skin, a dry cough, vaginal dryness, swollen glands in the cheeks or under the jaw, or numbness and tingling from nerve involvement. Symptoms vary a lot between people and can come and go.

How Sjögren's is diagnosed

There is no single test. A rheumatologist puts together your symptoms with other checks, which may include blood tests for particular antibodies (such as anti-Ro and anti-La), tests of tear production and eye surface health carried out by an eye specialist, measurement of saliva flow, and sometimes a small biopsy from the inside of the lip. Because symptoms overlap with lots of other causes of dryness, including menopause, some medicines and ageing, getting a diagnosis can take time.

Looking after dry eyes

Lubricating eye drops, gels and ointments are the mainstay. Preservative-free drops are often recommended if you use them many times a day. Gels or ointments at night can help if you wake with sore eyes.

  • Keep screens slightly below eye level and remember to blink fully.
  • Avoid sitting in draughts from fans, air conditioning or car vents.
  • Try wraparound glasses outdoors on windy days.
  • Ask your optometrist or GP about warm compresses and lid hygiene.
  • See an optician or eye service promptly for eye pain, light sensitivity or blurred vision that does not clear with blinking.

Looking after a dry mouth and teeth

Saliva protects teeth, so a dry mouth raises the risk of tooth decay, gum problems and mouth infections such as thrush.

  • Sip water regularly and keep a bottle by the bed.
  • Try saliva substitutes, gels or sprays, or sugar-free gum or lozenges to stimulate saliva.
  • Use a high-fluoride toothpaste if your dentist recommends one, and see your dentist and hygienist regularly.
  • Cut back on sugary snacks and acidic drinks between meals.
  • Tell your dentist and pharmacist that you have Sjögren's.

Treatment for the whole body

When joint pain, fatigue or other body-wide symptoms are a problem, a rheumatologist may suggest hydroxychloroquine, which needs regular eye checks, or other medicines for more serious organ involvement. Pacing, regular gentle exercise and good sleep habits help many people with fatigue. Medicines that cause dryness as a side effect are worth reviewing with your GP or pharmacist, but do not stop any prescribed medicine without advice.

When to seek medical advice

Tell your GP or rheumatology team about new or worsening symptoms. See a doctor promptly if a gland in your cheek, jaw or neck stays swollen for weeks, if you notice a new lump, unexplained weight loss or night sweats, or if you have persistent numbness, breathlessness or a new rash. Most of these have simple explanations, but they should be checked.

About this page

Written by Louis Maxwell, First Contact Practitioner (HCPC PH128483), and pending clinical review. This is general information, not a diagnosis. Always follow the advice of your own GP, physiotherapist or rheumatology team. For emergencies call 999; for urgent advice use NHS 111.

faqs.q: Is Sjögren's a type of arthritis?
faqs.a: Sjögren's is an autoimmune condition that mainly affects moisture-producing glands, but it often causes joint pain and can occur alongside rheumatoid arthritis or lupus. Rheumatologists usually look after it.

faqs.q: Can Sjögren's be cured?
faqs.a: There is no cure, but treatments for dryness, fatigue and joint pain can make a big difference to daily life, and many people live full lives with the right support.

faqs.q: Which eye drops are best for Sjögren's?
faqs.a: Preservative-free lubricating drops are often recommended for frequent use, with gels or ointments at night. Your optometrist, pharmacist or eye clinic can help you find the right type.

faqs.q: Why do I need to see the dentist more often?
faqs.a: Less saliva means less natural protection for your teeth and gums, so decay and gum problems can develop faster. Regular dental care and fluoride help prevent this.

faqs.q: Does Sjögren's cause tiredness?
faqs.a: Yes, fatigue is very common. Pacing, gentle regular exercise, good sleep habits and treating any linked problems, such as low thyroid or anaemia, can help.

/library/tens-machine.title: TENS Machine | Living With Arthritis UK
/library/tens-machine.question: TENS Machine
/library/tens-machine.answer: TENS stands for Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation. A TENS machine is a small, battery-operated device that delivers low-voltage electrical impulses through electrodes (sticky pads) placed on the skin near the area of pain. It is a non-invasive, drug-free method of pain relief that can be used at home.
/library/tens-machine.bodyHtml:
What is a TENS Machine?

TENS stands for Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation. A TENS machine is a small, battery-operated device that delivers low-voltage electrical impulses through electrodes (sticky pads) placed on the skin near the area of pain. It is a non-invasive, drug-free method of pain relief that can be used at home.

How Does it Work?

There are two main theories about how TENS works:

  • Gate control theory — the electrical impulses interfere with pain signals travelling to the brain, effectively "closing the gate" on pain perception
  • Endorphin release — the electrical stimulation triggers the release of the body's natural painkillers (endorphins and enkephalins)

What is it Used For?

  • Arthritis pain
  • Back pain
  • Knee pain
  • Sports injuries
  • Period pain
  • Labour pain during childbirth
  • Fibromyalgia
  • Endometriosis

How to Use a TENS Machine

Place the electrodes on clean, dry skin near the area of pain (not on broken skin, over the spine, or near the heart). Start at a low intensity and gradually increase until you feel a strong but comfortable tingling sensation. Sessions typically last 20–40 minutes. The device can be used multiple times a day.

Is it Safe?

TENS is generally safe for most people. However, it should not be used by people with pacemakers, epilepsy, or during pregnancy (except under medical supervision for labour pain). Always follow the manufacturer's instructions.

/library/vasculitis.title: Vasculitis: types, symptoms and treatment in one guide
/library/vasculitis.description: Vasculitis means inflamed blood vessels. This guide explains the main types from GCA to GPA, warning signs, blood and urine tests, treatment and living well.
/library/vasculitis.question: Vasculitis: types, symptoms and treatment explained
/library/vasculitis.answer: Vasculitis is a group of disorders characterised by inflammation of the blood vessels (arteries, veins, and capillaries). When blood vessel walls become inflamed, they can become weakened, stretch and bulge (aneurysm), or narrow and close off, restricting blood flow to organs and tissues. This can damage affected organ
/library/vasculitis.bodyHtml:
What is Vasculitis?

Vasculitis is a group of disorders characterised by inflammation of the blood vessels (arteries, veins, and capillaries). When blood vessel walls become inflamed, they can become weakened, stretch and bulge (aneurysm), or narrow and close off, restricting blood flow to organs and tissues. This can damage affected organs and may be life-threatening if not treated.

Types of Vasculitis

  • Giant cell arteritis (GCA) — affects large arteries, especially the temporal artery; most common in older adults
  • ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV) — includes granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) and microscopic polyangiitis (MPA)
  • IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura) — common in children
  • Polyarteritis nodosa
  • Behçet's disease
  • Kawasaki disease — in children

Symptoms

Symptoms vary depending on the type of vasculitis and the organs affected, but general signs include:

  • Fever and fatigue
  • Weight loss
  • Purpura — reddish-purple spots on the skin
  • Joint and muscle pain
  • Numbness or weakness
  • Organ-specific symptoms (e.g. blood in urine for kidney involvement, shortness of breath for lung involvement)

Treatment

Treatment depends on the type and severity. Most types are treated with corticosteroids to reduce inflammation. Immunosuppressant medications (such as cyclophosphamide, methotrexate, or rituximab) are used for severe or refractory disease. Early diagnosis and treatment are essential to prevent permanent organ damage.

Urgent warning signs

Some types of vasculitis can damage the eyes, kidneys, lungs or nerves quickly, so a few symptoms need urgent attention.

  • A new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw pain when chewing or any change in vision, especially if you are over 50: contact your GP the same day or call NHS 111. If you have lost vision, go to A&E. This can be giant cell arteritis.
  • Coughing up blood or sudden breathlessness: call 999 or go to A&E.
  • Blood in your urine, a new rash of purple spots, sudden numbness, weakness or foot drop, or feeling very unwell with fever: get medical help the same day.

The main types

Vasculitis is grouped by the size of the blood vessels involved.

  • Large vessels: giant cell arteritis (GCA), which affects arteries in the head and is the most common type in older adults and often overlaps with polymyalgia rheumatica; and Takayasu arteritis, which is rare and usually affects younger people.
  • Medium vessels: polyarteritis nodosa and Kawasaki disease, which mainly affects young children.
  • Small vessels: granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), microscopic polyangiitis and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA), often grouped as ANCA-associated vasculitis; and IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura), most common in children.
  • Vasculitis linked to other conditions, such as lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, infections including hepatitis, or certain medicines.

How it is diagnosed

Diagnosis combines your symptoms with tests. Blood tests look for inflammation (such as CRP and ESR), kidney function and particular antibodies. A urine dip test checks for blood or protein that may signal kidney involvement, and it is simple, quick and important. Scans such as ultrasound, CT or PET, and sometimes a biopsy of affected tissue, help confirm the type and extent. Because vasculitis can affect several organs, you may see more than one specialist.

Treatment

Treatment aims to switch off the inflammation quickly to protect organs, then keep it under control with the lowest effective treatment. Steroids are often used first because they work fast, with the dose reduced gradually over time. Other immune-calming medicines, such as methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate, rituximab or cyclophosphamide, may be added to control the disease and reduce the steroid dose. Some biologics are also used for specific types. Your team will explain the monitoring your medicines need, including blood tests, bone protection and infection precautions.

Living with vasculitis

Many people reach remission, although vasculitis can come back, so ongoing follow-up matters. Learn the early signs of a relapse that apply to you and how to contact your specialist team. Keep your vaccinations up to date as advised, particularly if you take immunosuppressants. Stay as active as you can, as this helps with fatigue, mood and bone health after steroids. Tell every health professional you see about your diagnosis and medicines, and carry a steroid card if you have been given one.

About this page

Written by Louis Maxwell, First Contact Practitioner (HCPC PH128483), and pending clinical review. This is general information, not a diagnosis. Always follow the advice of your own GP, physiotherapist or rheumatology team. For emergencies call 999; for urgent advice use NHS 111.

faqs.q: Is vasculitis a type of arthritis?
faqs.a: Vasculitis is inflammation of blood vessels rather than joints, but it can cause joint pain, and it is usually managed by rheumatology teams alongside other specialists.

faqs.q: Can vasculitis be cured?
faqs.a: Many people reach remission with treatment, and some stay well for long periods. Because it can return, regular follow-up and knowing your relapse warning signs are important.

faqs.q: Why do I need urine tests for vasculitis?
faqs.a: Some types of vasculitis affect the kidneys without causing symptoms at first. A simple urine test can pick up blood or protein early so treatment can be adjusted.

faqs.q: What is the link between PMR and giant cell arteritis?
faqs.a: They often occur together, especially in people over 50. Anyone with PMR should know the warning signs of GCA, such as new headache, jaw pain on chewing or vision changes, and seek same-day help if they appear.

faqs.q: Will I be on steroids for a long time?
faqs.a: Steroids are usually reduced gradually as the disease settles, and other medicines may be added to help lower the dose. Never stop steroids suddenly; follow your team's plan.

/library/ginger.description: A natural remedy with anti-inflammatory properties
/library/ginger.question: Ginger
/library/ginger.answer: Ginger (Zingiber officinale) is a flowering plant whose root has been used for thousands of years as both a culinary spice and a medicinal herb. It is native to Southeast Asia and is widely used in traditional medicine systems including Ayurveda and Chinese medicine. Its main bioactive compound, gingerol, is responsibl
/library/ginger.bodyHtml:
What is Ginger?

Ginger (Zingiber officinale) is a flowering plant whose root has been used for thousands of years as both a culinary spice and a medicinal herb. It is native to Southeast Asia and is widely used in traditional medicine systems including Ayurveda and Chinese medicine. Its main bioactive compound, gingerol, is responsible for most of its health benefits.

Health Benefits of Ginger

  • Anti-inflammatory — gingerol and shogaol have potent anti-inflammatory properties, which may benefit arthritis and other inflammatory conditions
  • Anti-nausea — very effective for nausea and vomiting, including morning sickness, motion sickness, and chemotherapy-induced nausea
  • Digestive aid — helps with indigestion, bloating, and stomach discomfort
  • Pain relief — some research suggests ginger may reduce muscle soreness and joint pain
  • Blood sugar control — may improve insulin sensitivity
  • Immune support — has antimicrobial and antioxidant properties

How to Use Ginger

  • Fresh ginger in cooking and smoothies
  • Ginger tea — steep fresh slices in hot water
  • Ginger supplements (capsules or extracts)
  • Dried ground ginger in recipes
  • Ginger ale (with real ginger content)

Is it Safe?

Ginger is generally safe when consumed in food amounts. High doses of ginger supplements may cause heartburn, diarrhoea, or stomach discomfort. People taking blood-thinning medications should consult their doctor before using ginger supplements, as it may increase bleeding risk.

/library/hypermobility.description: When joints move beyond their normal range
/library/hypermobility.question: Hypermobility
/library/hypermobility.answer: Hypermobility means that joints can move beyond the normal range of motion. Many people have hypermobile joints ("being double-jointed") without any problems, and some sports people and dancers even benefit from it. /library/hypermobility.bodyHtml:
What is Hypermobility?

Hypermobility means that joints can move beyond the normal range of motion. Many people have hypermobile joints ("being double-jointed") without any problems, and some sports people and dancers even benefit from it. However, for others, hypermobility is associated with pain, joint instability, and a range of other symptoms — a condition known as hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hEDS) or hypermobility spectrum disorder (HSD).

Why Does Hypermobility Cause Problems?

In people with symptomatic hypermobility, the connective tissue (which gives joints their stability) is more stretchy and lax than normal. This can lead to joints that are unstable, prone to sprains and dislocations, and surrounded by muscles that work harder to compensate — causing pain and fatigue.

Symptoms of Symptomatic Hypermobility

  • Widespread joint and muscle pain
  • Joint instability and frequent sprains or dislocations
  • Fatigue
  • Soft, stretchy skin
  • Digestive problems (IBS, acid reflux)
  • Postural tachycardia syndrome (POTS) — dizziness on standing
  • Anxiety and autonomic nervous system symptoms

Management

  • Physiotherapy — the most important treatment, focusing on strengthening muscles around unstable joints
  • Pain management — pacing, rest, and appropriate pain relief
  • Occupational therapy
  • Braces and supports for unstable joints
  • Proprioception training — to improve joint position sense

/library/achilles-tendonitis.description: Inflammation of the tendon connecting calf to heel
/library/achilles-tendonitis.question: Achilles Tendonitis
/library/achilles-tendonitis.answer: Achilles tendonitis (or tendinopathy) is inflammation or degeneration of the Achilles tendon — the large tendon at the back of the ankle that connects the calf muscles to the heel bone. It is one of the most common overuse injuries, particularly in runners and people who participate in sports involving jumping or sudde
/library/achilles-tendonitis.bodyHtml:
What is Achilles Tendonitis?

Achilles tendonitis (or tendinopathy) is inflammation or degeneration of the Achilles tendon — the large tendon at the back of the ankle that connects the calf muscles to the heel bone. It is one of the most common overuse injuries, particularly in runners and people who participate in sports involving jumping or sudden changes in direction.

Causes and Risk Factors

  • Overuse — a sudden increase in training intensity or volume
  • Tight or weak calf muscles
  • Flat feet or high arches
  • Running on hard or uneven surfaces
  • Inappropriate or worn-out footwear
  • Age — tendons become less flexible with age
  • Certain medications (fluoroquinolone antibiotics) can weaken tendons

Symptoms

  • Pain and stiffness along the Achilles tendon, especially in the morning
  • Pain that worsens with activity
  • Tenderness when touching the tendon
  • Swelling or thickening of the tendon
  • A crunching sensation when moving the ankle

Treatment

  • Rest from aggravating activity
  • Ice application
  • Eccentric heel drop exercises — the most evidence-based treatment
  • NSAIDs for pain and inflammation
  • Heel lifts in shoes to reduce tendon stress
  • Physiotherapy
  • Shockwave therapy for stubborn cases

/library/shoulder-pain.title: Shoulder Pain | Living With Arthritis UK
/library/shoulder-pain.question: Shoulder Pain
/library/shoulder-pain.answer: Shoulder pain is extremely common and can arise from a wide range of causes. The shoulder is the most mobile joint in the body, which makes it vulnerable to injury and instability. Pain can originate from the joint itself, the surrounding muscles, tendons, and bursa, or may even be referred from the neck or chest.
/library/shoulder-pain.bodyHtml:
Overview

Shoulder pain is extremely common and can arise from a wide range of causes. The shoulder is the most mobile joint in the body, which makes it vulnerable to injury and instability. Pain can originate from the joint itself, the surrounding muscles, tendons, and bursa, or may even be referred from the neck or chest.

Common Causes

  • Rotator cuff injuries — tears or tendonitis of the shoulder tendons
  • Frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis) — stiffness and pain that develops gradually
  • Impingement syndrome — tendons caught between shoulder bones
  • Bursitis — inflammation of the shoulder bursa
  • Acromioclavicular (AC) joint arthritis or injury
  • Shoulder dislocation or instability
  • Biceps tendonitis
  • Osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis
  • Referred pain from the neck (cervical radiculopathy)

Treatment

  • Rest and activity modification
  • Ice or heat therapy
  • NSAIDs
  • Physiotherapy — exercises to restore strength and range of motion
  • Corticosteroid injections
  • Surgery — for severe rotator cuff tears, instability, or advanced arthritis

Frozen Shoulder

Frozen shoulder typically develops in three stages: the freezing stage (increasing pain and stiffness), the frozen stage (reduced movement but less pain), and the thawing stage (gradual return of movement). It usually resolves on its own but can take 1–3 years. Physiotherapy and corticosteroid injections can speed recovery.

/library/hydroxychloroquine.title: Hydroxychloroquine: eye checks, side effects, what to expect
/library/hydroxychloroquine.description: Taking hydroxychloroquine for lupus or RA? How long it takes to work, common side effects, why yearly eye screening matters and tips for taking it well.
/library/hydroxychloroquine.question: Hydroxychloroquine: eye checks, side effects and what to expect
/library/hydroxychloroquine.answer: Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is a medication originally developed to prevent and treat malaria. It is now widely used as a disease-modifying drug for autoimmune and rheumatic conditions, including lupus (SLE), rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren's syndrome, and antiphospholipid syndrome (APS). Brand names include Plaquenil.
/library/hydroxychloroquine.bodyHtml:
What is Hydroxychloroquine?

Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is a medication originally developed to prevent and treat malaria. It is now widely used as a disease-modifying drug for autoimmune and rheumatic conditions, including lupus (SLE), rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren's syndrome, and antiphospholipid syndrome (APS). Brand names include Plaquenil.

How Does it Work?

In autoimmune conditions, hydroxychloroquine works by interfering with the function of immune cells involved in the inflammatory process. It alters the way cells process proteins and reduces the production of pro-inflammatory substances. The full benefit of hydroxychloroquine typically takes several months to become apparent.

Benefits

  • Reduces lupus flares and disease activity
  • Reduces joint pain and fatigue
  • Protects against organ damage in lupus (especially kidneys and blood vessels)
  • Reduces blood clotting risk in antiphospholipid syndrome
  • Has a relatively favourable safety profile compared to other immunosuppressants

Side Effects

  • Nausea and stomach upset — usually mild and improved by taking with food
  • Headache
  • Skin rash
  • Retinal toxicity — with very long-term use, there is a small risk of damage to the retina of the eye; regular eye check-ups are recommended

Eye Monitoring

Regular eye examinations are important for people taking hydroxychloroquine long-term. UK guidance from the Royal College of Ophthalmologists recommends a baseline eye check early in treatment and then yearly screening after five years of use (sooner if you have extra risk factors) to detect early signs of retinal toxicity.

Who is prescribed hydroxychloroquine

Hydroxychloroquine is one of the most widely used medicines in rheumatology. It is a first-choice treatment for lupus, where it helps prevent flares and protects organs over the long term, and it is often continued even when lupus is quiet. In rheumatoid arthritis it is used for milder disease or combined with other DMARDs such as methotrexate and sulfasalazine. It is also used for Sjögren's, palindromic rheumatism and some skin conditions. It is considered only mildly immune-suppressing, which is one reason it is so commonly used.

Taking it well

Hydroxychloroquine is a tablet taken once or twice a day. Your dose is worked out by your rheumatology team, partly based on your body weight, to keep the risk to your eyes low. Always take it as your team advises, and do not change the dose yourself.

  • Take it with food or a glass of milk if it upsets your stomach.
  • Leave a gap of several hours between hydroxychloroquine and indigestion remedies (antacids), which can reduce absorption.
  • Keep taking it even when you feel well; in lupus in particular, stopping can lead to flares.
  • If you miss a dose, check your leaflet or ask your pharmacist. Do not double up.
  • Keep tablets out of reach of children, as hydroxychloroquine is very dangerous in overdose.

How long it takes to work

Hydroxychloroquine works slowly. Some people notice an improvement in joint pain, rashes or tiredness after six to eight weeks, but it can take three to six months to reach its full effect. Your team may use other treatments to control symptoms in the meantime.

Eye screening explained

Long-term use of hydroxychloroquine can, in a small number of people, damage the retina at the back of the eye. Early damage usually causes no symptoms, which is why screening matters: it can pick up changes before your sight is affected, so the medicine can be stopped.

In the UK, screening is usually done in a hospital eye department with special scans of the retina and a visual field test. Most people have a baseline check early on and then yearly screening once they have taken hydroxychloroquine for five years. Screening starts sooner, after one year, if you have extra risk factors, such as reduced kidney function, a higher dose relative to your weight, or taking tamoxifen. Ask your team whether you have been referred.

A routine eye test at an optician is still worthwhile, but it does not replace hospital screening. Tell your team or an optometrist promptly if you notice difficulty reading, blurred or missing areas in your vision, or trouble seeing in dim light.

Other side effects

Most people take hydroxychloroquine with few problems. Side effects that can occur include:

  • Feeling sick, indigestion, tummy pain or diarrhoea, which often settle with time or taking tablets with food.
  • Headaches.
  • Skin rashes, itching or, over the long term, darkening of the skin in patches.
  • Increased sensitivity to sunlight, so use sun protection.
  • Low blood sugar in some people, especially those with diabetes; know the signs, such as shaking, sweating and confusion.
  • Rarely, effects on mood, hearing, muscles or heart rhythm. Tell your team about palpitations or fainting, and get urgent help for chest pain.

Pregnancy, breastfeeding, vaccines and alcohol

Hydroxychloroquine is usually continued during pregnancy and breastfeeding, particularly in lupus, because stopping it can lead to flares. Always discuss pregnancy plans with your team. It does not usually rule out vaccines, including most live vaccines, but check if you take other immune-suppressing medicines as well. There is no specific interaction with alcohol, but keep within UK low-risk drinking guidelines.

When to seek help

Contact your GP or rheumatology team the same day, or call NHS 111, if you have a widespread rash with fever or blistering, unexplained bruising, signs of low blood sugar that keep happening, or palpitations. Call 999 for chest pain, fainting or signs of a severe allergic reaction.

About this page

Written by Louis Maxwell, First Contact Practitioner (HCPC PH128483), and pending clinical review. This is general information, not a diagnosis. Always follow the advice of your own GP, physiotherapist or rheumatology team. For emergencies call 999; for urgent advice use NHS 111.

faqs.q: How long does hydroxychloroquine take to work?
faqs.a: Some people notice benefits after six to eight weeks, but it can take three to six months to reach its full effect.

faqs.q: Why do I need eye screening on hydroxychloroquine?
faqs.a: Long-term use can rarely damage the retina without early symptoms. Screening picks up changes early so the medicine can be stopped before sight is affected.

faqs.q: Can I take hydroxychloroquine during pregnancy?
faqs.a: It is usually continued during pregnancy and breastfeeding, especially in lupus. Discuss your plans with your rheumatology team.

faqs.q: Does hydroxychloroquine lower immunity?
faqs.a: It is only mildly immune-suppressing compared with many other arthritis medicines, and most people can have routine vaccines. Check with your team if you take other medicines too.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol on hydroxychloroquine?
faqs.a: There is no specific interaction, but keeping within UK low-risk drinking guidelines is sensible.

/library/musculoskeletal.description: Looking after your bones, muscles, and joints
/library/musculoskeletal.question: Musculoskeletal Health
/library/musculoskeletal.answer: The musculoskeletal system includes all the bones, muscles, tendons, ligaments, and joints in the body. /library/musculoskeletal.bodyHtml:
What is the Musculoskeletal System?

The musculoskeletal system includes all the bones, muscles, tendons, ligaments, and joints in the body. Together, these structures support the body, enable movement, and protect organs. Musculoskeletal conditions are the leading cause of disability worldwide and include conditions such as arthritis, back pain, osteoporosis, fibromyalgia, and sports injuries.

Common Musculoskeletal Conditions

  • Arthritis (osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis)
  • Back pain and neck pain
  • Osteoporosis
  • Fibromyalgia
  • Tendonitis and bursitis
  • Sports injuries (sprains, strains, fractures)
  • Hypermobility disorders
  • Carpal tunnel syndrome

Protecting Musculoskeletal Health

  • Stay active — regular weight-bearing and strength exercise maintains bone density and muscle strength
  • Maintain a healthy weight — reduces stress on joints
  • Eat well — a diet rich in calcium, vitamin D, and protein supports bone and muscle health
  • Protect your joints — use correct technique during exercise and at work
  • Posture — good posture reduces strain on the spine and joints
  • Don't smoke — smoking weakens bones and reduces blood supply to tissues
  • Warm up and cool down — before and after exercise

When to See a Doctor

See your GP if you have persistent joint or muscle pain that interferes with daily activities, pain that is worsening, swelling, redness, or warmth around a joint, or if you have had a fall or injury. Early assessment and treatment can prevent long-term damage.

/library/neck-pain.question: Neck Pain
/library/neck-pain.answer: Neck pain is one of the most common musculoskeletal problems and affects most people at some point in their lives. /library/neck-pain.bodyHtml:
Overview

Neck pain is one of the most common musculoskeletal problems and affects most people at some point in their lives. The neck (cervical spine) is made up of seven vertebrae (C1–C7) and is responsible for supporting the head and allowing a wide range of movement. This combination of mobility and the weight of the head makes the neck particularly susceptible to pain and injury.

Common Causes

  • Muscle strain — from poor posture, sleeping awkwardly, or prolonged sitting
  • Whiplash — from car accidents or sudden jerking movements
  • Cervical spondylosis — age-related wear and tear of the cervical discs and vertebrae
  • Herniated disc — a damaged disc pressing on a nerve
  • Cervical radiculopathy — nerve compression causing pain, numbness, or weakness radiating down the arm
  • Rheumatoid arthritis affecting the neck
  • Meningitis (rare but serious — stiff neck with fever requires urgent care)

Treatment

  • Pain relief — paracetamol or NSAIDs
  • Gentle movement — staying active and avoiding prolonged rest
  • Heat or ice therapy
  • Physiotherapy — exercises and manual therapy
  • Posture correction and ergonomic adjustments
  • TENS machine
  • Corticosteroid injections for nerve pain
  • Surgery — rarely needed

Prevention

  • Maintain good posture — especially when working at a computer
  • Take regular breaks from screens
  • Use a supportive pillow
  • Strengthen neck and upper back muscles
  • Avoid holding the phone between your shoulder and ear

/library/polymyalgia.description: Stiffness and pain in older adults
/library/polymyalgia.question: Polymyalgia Rheumatica
/library/polymyalgia.answer: Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) is an inflammatory condition that causes pain and stiffness in the shoulders, neck, upper arms, hips, and thighs. It almost exclusively affects people over 50 and is more common in women. PMR is one of the most common inflammatory conditions in older adults and, if treated promptly, usually
/library/polymyalgia.bodyHtml:
What is Polymyalgia Rheumatica?

Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) is an inflammatory condition that causes pain and stiffness in the shoulders, neck, upper arms, hips, and thighs. It almost exclusively affects people over 50 and is more common in women. PMR is one of the most common inflammatory conditions in older adults and, if treated promptly, usually responds very well to corticosteroid treatment.

Symptoms

  • Aching and stiffness in the shoulders, neck, upper arms, hips, and thighs
  • Morning stiffness lasting more than 45 minutes
  • Difficulty raising arms above shoulder height
  • Difficulty getting up from a chair
  • Fatigue
  • Low-grade fever
  • Unintentional weight loss

Diagnosis

Diagnosis is based on symptoms, age, and blood tests showing raised inflammatory markers (CRP and ESR). Other conditions (such as rheumatoid arthritis, myositis, and cancer) must be excluded first.

Link to Giant Cell Arteritis

About 15–20% of people with PMR also develop giant cell arteritis (GCA) — a serious inflammation of the arteries, particularly those supplying the eyes and brain. GCA can cause sudden vision loss and stroke. Symptoms of GCA include severe headache, jaw pain when chewing, scalp tenderness, and vision problems — these require urgent medical attention.

Treatment

PMR responds dramatically to low-dose prednisolone (a corticosteroid). Most people feel significantly better within days of starting treatment. Treatment usually continues for 1–2 years and is gradually tapered. Bone protection (calcium, vitamin D, and bisphosphonates) is important during long-term steroid use.

/library/selenium.title: Selenium | Living With Arthritis UK
/library/selenium.description: An essential trace mineral for immune and thyroid health
/library/selenium.question: Selenium
/library/selenium.answer: Selenium is an essential trace mineral that the body needs in small amounts to function properly. It is found naturally in soil and enters the food chain through plants and animals. Selenium plays a critical role in antioxidant defence, thyroid hormone metabolism, immune function, and DNA synthesis.
/library/selenium.bodyHtml:
What is Selenium?

Selenium is an essential trace mineral that the body needs in small amounts to function properly. It is found naturally in soil and enters the food chain through plants and animals. Selenium plays a critical role in antioxidant defence, thyroid hormone metabolism, immune function, and DNA synthesis.

Health Benefits

  • Antioxidant protection — selenium is a component of glutathione peroxidase, one of the body's most powerful antioxidant enzymes
  • Thyroid health — essential for thyroid hormone production and metabolism; deficiency can contribute to thyroid problems
  • Immune function — supports the immune response and may help protect against certain infections
  • Anti-inflammatory — some research suggests selenium may help reduce inflammation in conditions like rheumatoid arthritis
  • Cancer prevention — population studies suggest adequate selenium levels may lower cancer risk
  • Reproductive health — important for male fertility

Dietary Sources

  • Brazil nuts — the richest source (just 1–2 per day provides the daily requirement)
  • Fish and shellfish (tuna, sardines, oysters)
  • Meat and poultry
  • Eggs
  • Dairy products
  • Wholegrains (selenium content depends on soil levels)

Deficiency and Toxicity

Selenium deficiency is rare in the UK but can occur in people with malabsorption conditions. Symptoms include fatigue, hair loss, and weakened immunity. Too much selenium (selenium toxicity or selenosis) from high-dose supplements can cause nausea, hair loss, nail brittleness, and neurological problems. Do not exceed the recommended daily intake from supplements (400 micrograms/day for adults).

/library/adalimumab.description: A biologic treatment for inflammatory conditions
/library/adalimumab.question: Adalimumab
/library/adalimumab.answer: Adalimumab (brand name Humira, and several biosimilars) is a biologic medication — a type of treatment made from biological sources. /library/adalimumab.bodyHtml:
What is Adalimumab?

Adalimumab (brand name Humira, and several biosimilars) is a biologic medication — a type of treatment made from biological sources. It belongs to a class of drugs called TNF (tumour necrosis factor) inhibitors, or anti-TNF agents. TNF is a protein produced by the immune system that promotes inflammation. In conditions like rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, and Crohn's disease, TNF is overproduced, driving harmful inflammation. Adalimumab works by blocking TNF, reducing inflammation and preventing joint and tissue damage.

What is it Used For?

  • Rheumatoid arthritis
  • Psoriatic arthritis
  • Ankylosing spondylitis
  • Psoriasis
  • Crohn's disease
  • Ulcerative colitis
  • Uveitis (eye inflammation)
  • Hidradenitis suppurativa

How is it Given?

Adalimumab is given as a subcutaneous injection (under the skin), usually every two weeks. It comes as a pre-filled syringe or auto-injector pen for self-injection at home. Patients are trained by healthcare professionals on how to administer the injection safely.

Side Effects

  • Injection site reactions — redness, pain, or swelling
  • Increased risk of infections — particularly respiratory infections
  • Reactivation of latent tuberculosis (TB) — TB screening is required before starting
  • Rare: serious infections, certain cancers (especially lymphoma), heart failure

Monitoring

Regular blood tests and monitoring for signs of infection are essential. Live vaccinations should be avoided while on adalimumab. It should not be used in people with active infection, severe heart failure, or a history of certain cancers.

/library/lower-back-back.title: Lower Back Pain | Living With Arthritis UK
/library/lower-back-back.description: The most common cause of disability worldwide
/library/lower-back-back.question: Lower Back Pain
/library/lower-back-back.answer: Lower back pain affects up to 80% of people at some point in their lives and is the leading cause of disability worldwide. In most cases, it is not caused by a serious condition and improves with time and self-management. However, for some people it becomes chronic and significantly impacts quality of life.
/library/lower-back-back.bodyHtml:
Overview

Lower back pain affects up to 80% of people at some point in their lives and is the leading cause of disability worldwide. In most cases, it is not caused by a serious condition and improves with time and self-management. However, for some people it becomes chronic and significantly impacts quality of life.

Types of Lower Back Pain

  • Acute back pain — lasts less than 6 weeks, usually improves on its own
  • Subacute back pain — lasts 6–12 weeks
  • Chronic back pain — lasts more than 12 weeks
  • Specific back pain — caused by an identifiable condition (herniated disc, spinal stenosis, fracture)
  • Non-specific back pain — no clear structural cause (the most common type)

Common Causes

  • Muscle or ligament strain
  • Poor posture and sedentary behaviour
  • Herniated (slipped) disc
  • Spinal stenosis
  • Osteoarthritis of the spine
  • Ankylosing spondylitis
  • Kidney problems (referred pain)

Treatment

  • Stay active — rest is not recommended; gentle movement helps
  • Pain relief — paracetamol, NSAIDs, muscle relaxants
  • Hot or cold packs
  • Physiotherapy and exercise
  • Psychological support — CBT for chronic pain
  • Epidural steroid injections for nerve pain
  • Surgery — rarely needed (only for specific structural causes)

Red Flags

See a doctor urgently if back pain is accompanied by bladder or bowel problems, weakness or numbness in the legs, unexplained weight loss, fever, or follows a significant injury.

/library/msm.description: A sulphur-based supplement for joint health
/library/msm.question: MSM (Methylsulfonylmethane)
/library/msm.answer: Methylsulfonylmethane (MSM) is a naturally occurring sulphur compound found in plants, animals, and humans. It is a popular dietary supplement, often used to help manage joint pain, reduce inflammation, and support overall health. MSM is found naturally in small amounts in certain foods including garlic, onions, crucif
/library/msm.bodyHtml:
What is MSM?

Methylsulfonylmethane (MSM) is a naturally occurring sulphur compound found in plants, animals, and humans. It is a popular dietary supplement, often used to help manage joint pain, reduce inflammation, and support overall health. MSM is found naturally in small amounts in certain foods including garlic, onions, cruciferous vegetables, and milk, but the amounts in food are generally too small to have a therapeutic effect — hence the popularity of supplements.

How Does it Work?

MSM provides biologically active sulphur, which is an important component of proteins, collagen, and antioxidants in the body. Sulphur is essential for the formation and repair of connective tissues. MSM is also thought to have anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects, helping to reduce pain and inflammation in joints.

Potential Benefits

  • Reduces joint pain — research suggests MSM may significantly reduce pain in osteoarthritis
  • Decreases inflammation — may lower levels of inflammatory markers
  • Improves exercise recovery — may reduce muscle soreness after exercise
  • Supports skin health — may improve skin texture and reduce wrinkles
  • Immune support — antioxidant properties may help strengthen the immune system
  • Allergy relief — some evidence it may reduce allergic responses

Dosage and Safety

MSM is generally considered safe and well-tolerated. The typical dose used in research is 1–3 grams per day. Side effects are rare but can include mild digestive upset. There is currently no established tolerable upper limit, but high doses should be used with caution. MSM is generally safe alongside other medications, but it is always advisable to check with a pharmacist.

/library/colchicine.question: Colchicine
/library/colchicine.answer: Colchicine is a medication derived from the autumn crocus plant (Colchicum autumnale). It has been used for centuries to treat gout. Today, it is one of the most effective and recommended treatments for acute gout attacks and is also used to prevent recurrent gout. It is sometimes also used for other conditions includi
/library/colchicine.bodyHtml:
What is Colchicine?

Colchicine is a medication derived from the autumn crocus plant (Colchicum autumnale). It has been used for centuries to treat gout. Today, it is one of the most effective and recommended treatments for acute gout attacks and is also used to prevent recurrent gout. It is sometimes also used for other conditions including familial Mediterranean fever and pericarditis (inflammation around the heart).

How Does it Work?

Colchicine works by reducing the inflammation caused by uric acid crystals in the joint. It interferes with the migration of white blood cells (neutrophils) to the inflamed joint, thereby reducing the inflammatory response and the pain and swelling of a gout attack.

How to Take it

For an acute gout attack, colchicine is most effective when taken within the first 12–24 hours of an attack starting. The usual dose is 500 micrograms 2–3 times daily. For prevention of recurrent attacks, a low dose is taken daily (usually 500 micrograms once or twice daily).

Side Effects

  • Diarrhoea — the most common side effect, often dose-related
  • Nausea and stomach cramps
  • Vomiting
  • In overdose, colchicine can be very dangerous — store safely away from children

Interactions

Colchicine can interact with several medications, including statins, clarithromycin, and ciclosporin, potentially increasing the risk of serious side effects. Always inform your doctor and pharmacist of all medications you take.

/library/hip-pain.title: Hip Pain | Living With Arthritis UK
/library/hip-pain.question: Hip Pain
/library/hip-pain.answer: Hip pain is a very common complaint that can affect people of all ages. The hip is one of the largest and most important weight-bearing joints in the body. Hip pain can originate from structures within the joint itself (intra-articular) or from surrounding muscles, tendons, and bursae (extra-articular). It can also be
/library/hip-pain.bodyHtml:
Overview

Hip pain is a very common complaint that can affect people of all ages. The hip is one of the largest and most important weight-bearing joints in the body. Hip pain can originate from structures within the joint itself (intra-articular) or from surrounding muscles, tendons, and bursae (extra-articular). It can also be referred from the lower back or, less commonly, from the knee.

Common Causes

  • Osteoarthritis — the most common cause, especially in older adults
  • Hip bursitis — inflammation of the trochanteric bursa (outer hip)
  • Tendonitis — inflammation of hip tendons
  • Hip labral tear — damage to the cartilage lining the hip socket
  • Hip fracture — particularly in older adults with osteoporosis
  • Avascular necrosis — loss of blood supply to the femoral head
  • Rheumatoid arthritis
  • Referred pain from the lower back (sciatica)
  • IT band syndrome

Symptoms Indicating the Source

  • Groin pain — usually from inside the joint itself
  • Outer hip pain — often bursitis or tendonitis
  • Buttock pain — may be from the sacroiliac joint or referred from the back
  • Pain worse on stairs, getting up from a chair, or walking — suggests hip arthritis

Treatment

  • Rest and activity modification
  • NSAIDs for pain and inflammation
  • Physiotherapy — strengthening hip and gluteal muscles
  • Weight loss — reduces load on the hip joint
  • Corticosteroid or local anaesthetic injections
  • Hip replacement surgery — for severe osteoarthritis

/library/pins-needles.question: Pins and Needles in Hands
/library/pins-needles.answer: Pins and needles — medically known as paraesthesia — is a sensation of tingling, prickling, or numbness in the hands (or other body parts). /library/pins-needles.bodyHtml:
What Are Pins and Needles?

Pins and needles — medically known as paraesthesia — is a sensation of tingling, prickling, or numbness in the hands (or other body parts). Most people are familiar with the temporary "pins and needles" feeling after sitting in an awkward position that briefly cuts off blood supply or presses on a nerve. However, persistent or recurring pins and needles in the hands can indicate an underlying condition that needs assessment.

Common Causes

  • Carpal tunnel syndrome — the most common cause of pins and needles in the hands
  • Cervical radiculopathy — a pinched nerve in the neck
  • Cubital tunnel syndrome — ulnar nerve compression at the elbow
  • Peripheral neuropathy — nerve damage, often from diabetes
  • Raynaud's phenomenon
  • Vitamin B12 deficiency
  • Thoracic outlet syndrome
  • Multiple sclerosis (rarely)

Which Fingers Are Affected?

The pattern of pins and needles can help identify the cause:

  • Thumb, index, middle, and half of ring finger — carpal tunnel syndrome (median nerve)
  • Ring and little finger — cubital tunnel syndrome (ulnar nerve)
  • Whole hand — cervical radiculopathy or peripheral neuropathy

When to See a Doctor

See your GP if pins and needles in the hands are persistent, progressive, associated with weakness or loss of grip, or accompanied by other symptoms such as neck pain, visual changes, or balance problems.

/library/scleroderma.title: Scleroderma | Living With Arthritis UK
/library/scleroderma.description: A rare autoimmune condition affecting the skin and organs
/library/scleroderma.question: Scleroderma
/library/scleroderma.answer: Scleroderma (also known as systemic sclerosis) is a rare, chronic autoimmune condition in which the immune system triggers an overproduction of collagen, causing skin and connective tissues to harden and tighten. The name comes from the Greek words for hard (sclero) and skin (derma). Scleroderma can range from a mild c
/library/scleroderma.bodyHtml:
What is Scleroderma?

Scleroderma (also known as systemic sclerosis) is a rare, chronic autoimmune condition in which the immune system triggers an overproduction of collagen, causing skin and connective tissues to harden and tighten. The name comes from the Greek words for hard (sclero) and skin (derma). Scleroderma can range from a mild condition affecting only the skin to a severe systemic disease involving the lungs, kidneys, heart, and digestive system.

Types

  • Limited cutaneous scleroderma (lcSSc) — skin thickening limited to the hands, face, and lower arms; associated with CREST syndrome (Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Oesophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia)
  • Diffuse cutaneous scleroderma (dcSSc) — more widespread skin involvement and higher risk of organ involvement
  • Localised scleroderma (morphoea) — affects only the skin, not internal organs

Symptoms

  • Skin thickening, hardening, and tightening
  • Raynaud's phenomenon — almost universal in scleroderma
  • Puffy or swollen hands and fingers
  • Difficulty swallowing (oesophageal involvement)
  • Heartburn and reflux
  • Joint pain and stiffness
  • Lung fibrosis or pulmonary hypertension
  • Telangiectasia — small red spots from dilated blood vessels

Treatment

There is no cure for scleroderma. Treatment focuses on managing specific symptoms and preventing organ damage. This may include medications for Raynaud's, immunosuppressants for skin and lung disease, proton pump inhibitors for reflux, and specialist management for pulmonary hypertension or kidney crisis.

/library/aps.title: Antiphospholipid Syndrome (APS) | Living With Arthritis UK
/library/aps.question: Antiphospholipid Syndrome (APS)

/library/aps.bodyHtml:
What is APS?

Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS), also known as Hughes syndrome, is an autoimmune condition in which the immune system produces antibodies (antiphospholipid antibodies) that attack normal proteins in the blood, making it prone to clotting. This can lead to blood clots in arteries and veins and is a significant cause of strokes, deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism, and pregnancy complications. APS affects women more than men and is often associated with lupus.

Symptoms and Complications

  • Blood clots — in the legs (DVT), lungs (pulmonary embolism), brain (stroke or TIA)
  • Recurrent miscarriages — APS is a leading treatable cause of recurrent pregnancy loss
  • Livedo reticularis — a mottled, net-like discolouration of the skin
  • Low platelet count (thrombocytopenia)
  • Headaches and migraines
  • Memory problems and cognitive difficulties
  • Heart valve problems

Diagnosis

APS is diagnosed when someone has had a clot or pregnancy complication AND tests positive for antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibodies, or anti-beta2 glycoprotein-I antibodies) on at least two separate occasions, 12 weeks apart.

Treatment

  • Anticoagulation (blood thinning) — warfarin or newer anticoagulants (DOACs) to prevent clots
  • Low-dose aspirin — particularly for pregnancy-related APS
  • Hydroxychloroquine — to reduce antibody levels
  • Heparin injections during pregnancy to prevent miscarriage

/library/arthritis-symptoms.title: Arthritis symptoms UK: pain, stiffness and when to see a GP
/library/arthritis-symptoms.description: How arthritis symptoms present in the UK — joint pain, morning stiffness, swelling and fatigue — and which patterns need a prompt GP appointment.
/library/arthritis-symptoms.question: Arthritis symptoms: what to notice before a diagnosis has a name
/library/arthritis-symptoms.answer: Arthritis can present in many different ways depending on the type. Recognising symptoms early is important as it enables earlier diagnosis and treatment, which can prevent joint damage and improve long-term outcomes. While symptoms vary by type, there are many common features across all forms of arthritis.
/library/arthritis-symptoms.bodyHtml:
Overview

Arthritis can present in many different ways depending on the type. Recognising symptoms early is important as it enables earlier diagnosis and treatment, which can prevent joint damage and improve long-term outcomes. While symptoms vary by type, there are many common features across all forms of arthritis.

Joint Pain

Pain is the most universal symptom of arthritis. It may be a dull, aching, or sharp pain that is present constantly or comes and goes. The pattern of pain can help identify the type — for example, osteoarthritis pain typically worsens with activity and eases with rest, while inflammatory arthritis pain (such as rheumatoid arthritis) is often worse after rest and improves with movement.

Stiffness

Joint stiffness — particularly morning stiffness — is a hallmark feature of inflammatory arthritis. In rheumatoid arthritis, morning stiffness lasts more than 30 minutes to an hour. In osteoarthritis, stiffness is usually shorter-lived (less than 30 minutes).

Swelling

Inflammation in and around a joint causes swelling. The joint may feel warm to the touch and appear visibly enlarged. In some types of arthritis (such as psoriatic arthritis), entire digits may be swollen (dactylitis).

Reduced Range of Movement

Inflamed or damaged joints become stiff and difficult to move through their full range. This can make everyday tasks like opening jars, climbing stairs, or buttoning clothing difficult.

Fatigue

Inflammatory arthritis is often accompanied by significant fatigue — a deep, persistent tiredness that is not relieved by sleep. This is related to the systemic inflammatory process and can be as debilitating as the joint symptoms.

Other Symptoms

  • Redness and warmth over the joint
  • Creaking or grinding sounds (crepitus)
  • Deformity of joints in long-standing disease
  • Skin rashes (in psoriatic arthritis or lupus)
  • Eye problems (in ankylosing spondylitis or psoriatic arthritis)

Inflammatory versus wear-and-tear patterns

Two patterns help a GP decide what to do next. Osteoarthritis pain usually builds over months or years, worsens with use, and stiffness lasts under half an hour. Inflammatory arthritis (RA, PsA, lupus, AS) more often causes prolonged morning stiffness, warmth, swelling of several joints, and fatigue that feels systemic. Either pattern deserves a GP visit if it is limiting work, sleep or walking — but inflammatory features should be mentioned explicitly because NICE expects earlier rheumatology referral.

Symptoms that should not wait

Book urgently if a single joint is suddenly hot, red and you cannot weight-bear; if you have a high fever with joint pain; or if a child has a persistent limp. Those can be infection or, in children, juvenile idiopathic arthritis. For everyone else, more than a few weeks of joint swelling, stiffness lasting over 30 minutes, or unexplained fatigue with pain is enough to justify a routine GP appointment and basic blood tests.

/library/naproxen-500mg.question: Naproxen 500mg
/library/naproxen-500mg.answer: Naproxen 500mg is a prescription-strength dose of the NSAID naproxen. While lower doses (220–250mg) are available over the counter for mild pain and fever, the 500mg dose is typically prescribed by a doctor for more significant inflammatory conditions such as arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, gout, and moderate to sev
/library/naproxen-500mg.bodyHtml:
What is Naproxen 500mg?

Naproxen 500mg is a prescription-strength dose of the NSAID naproxen. While lower doses (220–250mg) are available over the counter for mild pain and fever, the 500mg dose is typically prescribed by a doctor for more significant inflammatory conditions such as arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, gout, and moderate to severe musculoskeletal pain.

When is it Prescribed?

  • Rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis
  • Gout attacks
  • Ankylosing spondylitis
  • Bursitis and tendonitis
  • Post-surgical pain and inflammation
  • Severe menstrual pain
  • Acute musculoskeletal injuries

Dosage

The usual starting dose is 500mg twice daily (morning and evening), giving a total of 1,000mg per day. Some conditions may be treated with 500mg three times daily. The maximum daily dose on prescription is 1,500mg. Always take it with food or milk to reduce the risk of stomach upset.

Stomach Protection

Because naproxen 500mg is a higher dose taken regularly, your doctor will often prescribe a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) such as omeprazole alongside it to protect the stomach lining and reduce the risk of stomach ulcers.

Important Considerations

  • Do not combine with other NSAIDs (ibuprofen, aspirin for pain)
  • Monitor blood pressure — NSAIDs can raise it
  • Use with caution in older adults and those with kidney or heart problems
  • Not suitable for people with active stomach ulcers

/library/shoulder-exercises.title: Shoulder Exercises | Living With Arthritis UK
/library/shoulder-exercises.question: Shoulder Exercises
/library/shoulder-exercises.answer: Exercise is one of the most important treatments for shoulder problems including rotator cuff injuries, frozen shoulder, impingement syndrome, bursitis, and shoulder arthritis. Strengthening the muscles around the shoulder joint improves stability, reduces pain, and helps restore normal movement. Physiotherapy-guided e
/library/shoulder-exercises.bodyHtml:
Why Exercise the Shoulder?

Exercise is one of the most important treatments for shoulder problems including rotator cuff injuries, frozen shoulder, impingement syndrome, bursitis, and shoulder arthritis. Strengthening the muscles around the shoulder joint improves stability, reduces pain, and helps restore normal movement. Physiotherapy-guided exercises are the cornerstone of shoulder rehabilitation.

Key Muscle Groups to Target

  • Rotator cuff muscles — supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis
  • Deltoid — the main shoulder muscle
  • Trapezius and rhomboids — upper back muscles that support shoulder blade movement
  • Serratus anterior — stabilises the shoulder blade

Effective Shoulder Exercises

  • Pendulum exercises — let the arm hang and make small circular movements; helps in frozen shoulder
  • External rotation — with an elastic band, rotate the arm outwards; strengthens the rotator cuff
  • Shoulder press — using light weights, press overhead; builds deltoid strength
  • Rows — pull a resistance band or cable towards you; strengthens upper back and rear shoulder
  • Wall slides — slide arms up a wall while maintaining contact; improves shoulder blade mechanics
  • Doorway stretch — stretches the chest and anterior shoulder to improve posture

Safety Tips

  • Always warm up before exercising
  • Start gently and progress gradually
  • Stop any exercise that causes significant pain
  • Seek guidance from a physiotherapist for personalised advice

/library/what-is-gout.question: What is Gout?
/library/what-is-gout.answer: Gout is a form of inflammatory arthritis that develops when there is too much uric acid in the blood (hyperuricaemia). Uric acid is produced when the body breaks down purines — substances found naturally in the body and in many foods. /library/what-is-gout.bodyHtml:
Overview

Gout is a form of inflammatory arthritis that develops when there is too much uric acid in the blood (hyperuricaemia). Uric acid is produced when the body breaks down purines — substances found naturally in the body and in many foods. When uric acid levels are too high, it can crystallise and deposit in joints as needle-like monosodium urate crystals, triggering intense inflammation and pain. Gout is more common in men and becomes increasingly common with age. It affects around 2.5% of the UK population.

Why Does Uric Acid Build Up?

Uric acid levels rise either because the body produces too much of it, or the kidneys do not excrete enough. Several factors contribute:

  • Diet — high intake of red meat, organ meats, shellfish, alcohol, and sugary drinks
  • Obesity
  • Kidney disease — reduced kidney function means less uric acid is excreted
  • Genetic factors
  • Certain medications — diuretics (water tablets), low-dose aspirin, ciclosporin
  • Dehydration

Stages of Gout

  • Asymptomatic hyperuricaemia — high uric acid but no symptoms yet
  • Acute gout — sudden, severe joint attacks
  • Intercritical gout — periods between attacks with no symptoms
  • Chronic tophaceous gout — persistent gout with visible deposits (tophi) if untreated

Treatment Goals

The two main goals of gout treatment are: (1) treating acute attacks promptly with NSAIDs, colchicine, or corticosteroids, and (2) preventing future attacks and lowering uric acid levels in the long term with medications like allopurinol or febuxostat, combined with lifestyle changes.

/library/kawasaki.description: A childhood vasculitis affecting coronary arteries
/library/kawasaki.question: Kawasaki Disease
/library/kawasaki.answer: Kawasaki disease is a rare but serious condition primarily affecting children under 5 years of age. It is a form of vasculitis — inflammation of blood vessels — that mainly affects medium-sized arteries, including the coronary arteries (the arteries supplying the heart). Without prompt treatment, Kawasaki disease can c
/library/kawasaki.bodyHtml:
What is Kawasaki Disease?

Kawasaki disease is a rare but serious condition primarily affecting children under 5 years of age. It is a form of vasculitis — inflammation of blood vessels — that mainly affects medium-sized arteries, including the coronary arteries (the arteries supplying the heart). Without prompt treatment, Kawasaki disease can cause coronary artery aneurysms, which may lead to heart attack. It is the most common cause of acquired heart disease in children in developed countries.

Symptoms (Five Main Features)

A diagnosis of Kawasaki disease requires fever lasting 5 or more days plus four of the following five features:

  • Rash — a widespread red rash on the body
  • Red, cracked lips and a strawberry tongue
  • Swollen lymph nodes in the neck (cervical lymphadenopathy)
  • Red, swollen hands and feet, sometimes with peeling of the skin
  • Red, inflamed eyes (conjunctivitis) without discharge

Treatment

Treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) and high-dose aspirin is very effective when given early (within 10 days of fever onset). IVIG dramatically reduces the risk of coronary artery complications. Aspirin is later reduced to a low dose to prevent blood clots. Most children make a full recovery with timely treatment.

Long-term Follow-up

Children who develop coronary artery aneurysms require long-term cardiac follow-up. Those with no cardiac complications generally have an excellent prognosis. Early recognition and treatment are the most critical factors in preventing serious heart complications.

/library/british-supplements.description: Understanding dietary supplements available in the UK
/library/british-supplements.question: British Supplements
/library/british-supplements.answer: Dietary supplements are widely used in the UK to support health and wellbeing. They include vitamins, minerals, herbal products, amino acids, and other substances. In the UK, supplements are regulated as food products rather than medicines, meaning they do not need to prove their effectiveness before being sold — thoug
/library/british-supplements.bodyHtml:
Overview

Dietary supplements are widely used in the UK to support health and wellbeing. They include vitamins, minerals, herbal products, amino acids, and other substances. In the UK, supplements are regulated as food products rather than medicines, meaning they do not need to prove their effectiveness before being sold — though they must be safe and labelled accurately.

Most Commonly Used Supplements in the UK

  • Vitamin D — particularly important in the UK where sunlight is limited, especially in autumn and winter; NICE recommends 10 micrograms daily for everyone
  • Omega-3 fish oils — for heart health and anti-inflammatory effects
  • Vitamin C — antioxidant and immune support
  • Magnesium — muscle function, sleep, and nerve health
  • Glucosamine and chondroitin — for joint health
  • Turmeric/curcumin — anti-inflammatory
  • Collagen peptides — for skin and joint health
  • B vitamins — energy metabolism and nervous system function
  • Calcium — bone health
  • Probiotics — gut health and immunity

Quality and Regulation

In the UK, look for supplements approved by the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) or bearing quality marks such as the Informed Sport logo (for tested purity) or the Soil Association mark (for organic). Third-party testing provides greater assurance of quality and label accuracy.

Are Supplements Safe?

Most supplements are safe when taken as directed. However, some can interact with prescribed medications, and very high doses of certain vitamins and minerals can be harmful. Always tell your doctor and pharmacist about any supplements you are taking. Supplements should complement — not replace — a balanced diet and prescribed treatments.

/library/plantar-fasciitis-treatment.title: Plantar Fasciitis Treatment | Living With Arthritis UK
/library/plantar-fasciitis-treatment.description: Evidence-based approaches to heel pain relief
/library/plantar-fasciitis-treatment.question: Plantar Fasciitis Treatment
/library/plantar-fasciitis-treatment.answer: Most cases of plantar fasciitis resolve with conservative treatment, although it can take several months. The key is consistency and patience. A combination of different approaches tends to be most effective.
/library/plantar-fasciitis-treatment.bodyHtml:
Overview of Treatment

Most cases of plantar fasciitis resolve with conservative treatment, although it can take several months. The key is consistency and patience. A combination of different approaches tends to be most effective.

Stretching Exercises

Stretching is one of the most effective treatments. The most important stretches include:

  • Plantar fascia stretch — pull the toes back towards the shin and hold for 30 seconds before taking your first steps in the morning
  • Calf stretch — stand facing a wall and stretch each calf with knee straight and then bent (to target both calf muscles)
  • Towel stretch — loop a towel around the foot and gently pull the toes towards you while lying down

Footwear and Orthotics

  • Wear supportive shoes with good cushioning and arch support at all times — avoid walking barefoot, especially on hard floors
  • Custom or over-the-counter orthotics (shoe insoles) can help distribute pressure evenly
  • Night splints hold the foot in a flexed position during sleep, keeping the plantar fascia gently stretched

Pain Relief and Anti-inflammatory Measures

  • NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) — reduce pain and inflammation
  • Ice massage — roll a frozen water bottle under the foot for 10–15 minutes
  • Rest — reduce high-impact activities

Medical Treatments

  • Corticosteroid injections — effective for short-term relief; multiple injections can weaken the fascia
  • Extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT) — for chronic cases unresponsive to other treatments
  • Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injections — emerging evidence of benefit
  • Surgery (plantar fasciotomy) — a last resort, rarely needed

/library/aspirin.question: Aspirin
/library/aspirin.answer: Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) is one of the oldest and most widely used medications in the world. It belongs to the NSAID class and has three main effects: it relieves mild to moderate pain, reduces fever, and reduces inflammation. At low doses (75mg), it also has blood-thinning (antiplatelet) properties, which is why
/library/aspirin.bodyHtml:
What is Aspirin?

Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) is one of the oldest and most widely used medications in the world. It belongs to the NSAID class and has three main effects: it relieves mild to moderate pain, reduces fever, and reduces inflammation. At low doses (75mg), it also has blood-thinning (antiplatelet) properties, which is why it is widely used to prevent heart attacks and strokes in people at risk.

Uses of Aspirin

  • Pain relief — headaches, toothache, period pain, muscle pain (300–900mg doses)
  • Fever reduction
  • Prevention of heart attacks and strokes — low-dose aspirin (75mg) prevents platelets from clumping together and forming clots
  • Treatment of acute heart attack — 300mg chewed immediately as first aid
  • Antiphospholipid syndrome
  • Kawasaki disease
  • Pre-eclampsia prevention in pregnancy (under medical supervision)

Who Should Not Take Aspirin?

  • Children under 16 (risk of Reye's syndrome)
  • People with stomach ulcers or bleeding disorders
  • Those with aspirin allergy or asthma triggered by NSAIDs
  • Pregnant women (except low-dose under medical supervision)

Side Effects

  • Stomach irritation and indigestion
  • Increased bleeding risk
  • Stomach ulcers with long-term use
  • Tinnitus at high doses

/library/turmeric-benefits.answer: Curcumin — the active compound in turmeric — is one of the most potent natural anti-inflammatory substances known. Research has shown it can inhibit several molecular pathways involved in chronic inflammation, including NF-ÎºB, one of the key drivers of inflammation in arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, and other c
/library/turmeric-benefits.bodyHtml:
Anti-inflammatory Effects

Curcumin — the active compound in turmeric — is one of the most potent natural anti-inflammatory substances known. Research has shown it can inhibit several molecular pathways involved in chronic inflammation, including NF-ÎºB, one of the key drivers of inflammation in arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, and other conditions. Some studies suggest curcumin may rival the anti-inflammatory power of some NSAIDs, without the same side effect profile.

Joint Pain and Arthritis

Multiple clinical trials have shown that curcumin supplementation can significantly reduce pain and improve function in people with knee osteoarthritis. A 2021 review found curcumin was as effective as ibuprofen for knee arthritis pain with fewer gastrointestinal side effects. It may also benefit people with rheumatoid arthritis by reducing inflammatory markers.

Digestive Health

Turmeric has been used traditionally for digestive complaints for centuries. Modern research supports its use in irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). It may help reduce bloating, gas, and discomfort in IBS, and animal studies suggest curcumin may help reduce gut inflammation in Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.

Brain and Mental Health

Curcumin crosses the blood-brain barrier and has shown potential neuroprotective effects in research. Studies suggest it may boost levels of BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor), a growth hormone important for brain function, and may have antidepressant effects comparable to certain medications in some studies.

Heart Health

Curcumin may improve several heart disease risk factors, including reducing LDL cholesterol oxidation, improving endothelial (blood vessel lining) function, and reducing inflammation — all important factors in cardiovascular disease prevention.

/library/back-exercises.description: Strengthening and stretching for a healthy back
/library/back-exercises.question: Back Exercises
/library/back-exercises.answer: Exercise is one of the most effective treatments for back pain. Staying active — rather than resting in bed — speeds recovery from acute back pain and reduces the risk of it becoming chronic. For chronic back pain, regular exercise is the cornerstone of management, helping to strengthen the muscles that support the spi
/library/back-exercises.bodyHtml:
Why Exercise Helps Back Pain

Exercise is one of the most effective treatments for back pain. Staying active — rather than resting in bed — speeds recovery from acute back pain and reduces the risk of it becoming chronic. For chronic back pain, regular exercise is the cornerstone of management, helping to strengthen the muscles that support the spine, improve flexibility, and reduce pain through the release of natural endorphins.

Core Strengthening Exercises

  • Pelvic tilts — lie on your back with knees bent, gently flatten the lower back against the floor and hold for 5–10 seconds
  • Dead bugs — lie on your back, raise arms and legs, then lower opposite arm and leg alternately while keeping the back flat
  • Bird dog — on hands and knees, extend opposite arm and leg while keeping the back straight
  • Bridge — lie on your back with knees bent, lift the hips off the floor and hold for 5–10 seconds
  • Plank — hold a straight position on forearms and toes, building up time gradually

Stretching Exercises

  • Knee to chest stretch — lie on your back, pull one knee gently to the chest and hold
  • Cat-cow stretch — on hands and knees, alternate arching and rounding the back
  • Child's pose — sit back on heels, stretch arms forward along the floor
  • Piriformis stretch — lie on your back, cross one ankle over the opposite knee and gently pull

Aerobic Exercise

Walking, swimming, and cycling are excellent low-impact aerobic exercises that maintain spinal health and overall fitness without putting excessive stress on the back. Aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate activity per week.

/library/mtx-methotrexal.question: MTX (Methotrexate) — Patient Guide
/library/mtx-methotrexal.answer: Methotrexate (often referred to as MTX) is one of the most widely used disease-modifying treatments for inflammatory arthritis and other autoimmune conditions. For many people, it becomes a long-term part of their health management. Understanding what to expect and how to manage treatment safely is important for gettin
/library/mtx-methotrexal.bodyHtml:
Overview

Methotrexate (often referred to as MTX) is one of the most widely used disease-modifying treatments for inflammatory arthritis and other autoimmune conditions. For many people, it becomes a long-term part of their health management. Understanding what to expect and how to manage treatment safely is important for getting the best results.

The Weekly Dose — Why It Matters

One of the most important things to remember about methotrexate for arthritis is that it is taken ONCE A WEEK, not every day. Taking it every day instead of weekly has caused serious accidental harm. Write the day on a calendar, set a phone alarm, or use a weekly pill organiser to help remember. Do not take it more often than prescribed.

Folic Acid — Take it Every Week

Folic acid is always prescribed alongside methotrexate to reduce side effects (especially nausea and mouth sores). It is taken on a different day to methotrexate — typically 5mg once a week. Do not skip folic acid doses.

Blood Monitoring

Regular blood tests are essential throughout methotrexate treatment. Tests monitor the liver (liver enzymes), kidneys, and blood cells. Initially, tests are done every 2–4 weeks and can be spaced to 3-monthly once stable. Never miss monitoring appointments — they detect any problems early.

Alcohol

Alcohol must be avoided or strictly limited (ideally no more than 1–2 units per week, and no binge drinking) because methotrexate and alcohol are both processed by the liver and can cause liver damage together.

Contraception

Both men and women must use reliable contraception while on methotrexate. Women must avoid pregnancy for at least 3 months after stopping. Men should avoid fathering a child for at least 3 months after stopping.
