/library/naproxen-adverse.question: Naproxen Adverse Effects
/library/naproxen-adverse.answer: While naproxen is an effective anti-inflammatory and painkiller, like all NSAIDs it carries a risk of side effects. Most people tolerate naproxen well, especially when taken at the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible time. However, it is important to be aware of potential adverse effects, particularly with
/library/naproxen-adverse.bodyHtml:
Overview

While naproxen is an effective anti-inflammatory and painkiller, like all NSAIDs it carries a risk of side effects. Most people tolerate naproxen well, especially when taken at the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible time. However, it is important to be aware of potential adverse effects, particularly with long-term use.

Gastrointestinal (Stomach and Gut) Effects

This is the most common category of naproxen side effects:

Always take naproxen with food or milk. A proton pump inhibitor (e.g. omeprazole) is usually co-prescribed for long-term use.

  • Indigestion, heartburn, and stomach pain
  • Nausea
  • Stomach ulcers — naproxen reduces the stomach lining's protective mucus
  • Gastrointestinal bleeding — a serious risk with long-term use; warning signs include dark, tarry stools or vomiting blood

Cardiovascular Effects

  • Raised blood pressure
  • Increased risk of heart attack and stroke with long-term high-dose use — particularly in people who already have cardiovascular disease
  • Fluid retention and ankle swelling

Kidney Effects

  • Reduced kidney function — particularly with dehydration, in older adults, or in those with existing kidney disease
  • Sodium and fluid retention worsening kidney function

Other Side Effects

  • Headache and dizziness
  • Skin rashes and photosensitivity
  • Tinnitus (ringing in the ears)
  • Allergic reactions — more common in people with aspirin-sensitive asthma

Minimising Risks

  • Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time
  • Always take with food
  • Stay well hydrated
  • Have regular blood pressure and kidney function checks if using long-term
  • Report any new or worsening symptoms to your doctor

/library/osteoporosis-osteoporosis.question: Osteoporosis — In Depth
/library/osteoporosis-osteoporosis.answer: Bone is a living tissue that is constantly being renewed. Old bone is removed by cells called osteoclasts and new bone is formed by osteoblasts. /library/osteoporosis-osteoporosis.bodyHtml:
Understanding Bone Structure and Loss

Bone is a living tissue that is constantly being renewed. Old bone is removed by cells called osteoclasts and new bone is formed by osteoblasts. In youth, bone is formed faster than it is broken down, reaching peak bone mass in the late 20s. After 35, bone density naturally starts to decline. In osteoporosis, bone is broken down faster than it is replaced, leaving bones weak and fragile.

The Menopause Connection

The most significant risk factor for osteoporosis in women is the menopause. Oestrogen plays a crucial role in maintaining bone density by inhibiting osteoclast activity. After the menopause, oestrogen levels fall sharply, accelerating bone loss. Women can lose up to 20% of their bone density in the 5–7 years following menopause.

Diagnosing Osteoporosis: The T-score

A DEXA scan measures bone mineral density (BMD) and compares it to that of a healthy young adult. The result is expressed as a T-score:

  • T-score above -1: Normal bone density
  • T-score between -1 and -2.5: Osteopenia (low bone density, precursor to osteoporosis)
  • T-score below -2.5: Osteoporosis

Treatment in Detail

  • Bisphosphonates (alendronic acid, risedronate) — inhibit osteoclast activity; most commonly prescribed; taken as a weekly tablet
  • Denosumab (Prolia) — a biologic injection given every 6 months; an alternative for those who cannot tolerate bisphosphonates
  • Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) — effective for postmenopausal women; also treats menopausal symptoms
  • Teriparatide — an anabolic treatment that stimulates bone formation; used in severe osteoporosis
  • Calcium (1,000–1,200mg/day) and Vitamin D (800–1,000 IU/day) supplements — essential alongside all treatments

Fall Prevention

Since fractures occur when fragile bones are subjected to trauma (usually falls), fall prevention is as important as bone-strengthening. Balance exercises (such as tai chi), reviewing medications that cause dizziness, improving home safety (removing trip hazards, adding grab rails), and wearing appropriate footwear all significantly reduce fracture risk.

Contrary to the outdated advice that peop

/library/manchester-marathon.about: Exercise and Arthritis: Running and Physical Activity
/library/manchester-marathon.bodyHtml:
Exercise as Medicine

For most people with arthritis, regular physical activity is one of the most beneficial things they can do. Exercise strengthens the muscles around joints, reduces pain, improves joint function and flexibility, lifts mood, controls weight, and helps prevent disease progression. Contrary to the outdated advice that people with arthritis should rest, exercise is now firmly recommended by NICE and Arthritis UK.

Can You Run with Arthritis?

Many people with arthritis, including osteoarthritis of the knee, continue to run. Research has shown that regular runners do not have higher rates of knee arthritis than non-runners — and some studies suggest running may actually protect joints by maintaining cartilage health. If you have arthritis and want to run, the key is to:

  • Start slowly and build up gradually
  • Wear supportive running shoes
  • Run on softer surfaces (grass or trail rather than concrete)
  • Incorporate rest days and low-impact cross-training (cycling, swimming)
  • Strengthen supporting muscles through resistance training
  • Listen to your body and reduce intensity during flares

Goal-Setting with Arthritis

Setting achievable goals — such as completing a charity 5K, parkrun, or even a half marathon — can be a powerful motivator for people with arthritis. Many people with inflammatory arthritis have completed marathons and triathlons. The key is working with your healthcare team and finding the activity level that works for your condition.

Types of Recommended Exercise

  • Aerobic (cardiovascular): walking, swimming, cycling, aqua aerobics
  • Strengthening: resistance bands, weights, bodyweight exercises
  • Flexibility: yoga, Pilates, stretching
  • Balance: tai chi, balance boards

/library/hypermobility-and.bodyHtml:
The Hypermobility Spectrum

Hypermobility spectrum disorders (HSD) and hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hEDS) are a continuum of conditions characterised by joint hypermobility (excessive range of movement), pain, and systemic symptoms. They are more common than previously recognised and are thought to affect 1 in 500 people, though many remain undiagnosed. The conditions predominantly affect women and often run in families.

Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (hEDS)

hEDS is the most common type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, a group of inherited connective tissue disorders. In hEDS, the connective tissue that gives joints their structure is more elastic than normal, leading to widespread hypermobility, joint instability, and a range of systemic features. Diagnosis requires meeting specific clinical criteria including evidence of generalised hypermobility, symptoms of joint instability and pain, and systemic features.

Associated Conditions

HSD and hEDS are frequently associated with:

  • Postural tachycardia syndrome (POTS) — dizziness and rapid heart rate on standing
  • Mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS) — allergic-type reactions
  • Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and gut dysmotility
  • Anxiety and depression
  • Fatigue — often severe
  • Chronic pain

Management

There is no cure but symptoms can be managed effectively. Key approaches include physiotherapy (the most important treatment), pain management, cardiovascular support for POTS, pacing strategies for fatigue, occupational therapy, and psychological support. Referral to a specialist centre with experience in hypermobility disorders is beneficial for complex cases.

/library/discomfort-knee.bodyHtml:
Overview

Discomfort or pain in the knee joint is one of the most frequent reasons people visit their GP or physiotherapist. The knee is a complex joint, made up of bone, cartilage, ligaments, tendons, and fluid-filled sacs (bursae) — any of which can become a source of pain. Understanding the character and location of knee discomfort can help identify its likely cause.

Types of Knee Discomfort

  • Sharp pain — may suggest a meniscus tear, ligament injury, or loose body in the joint
  • Dull, aching pain — often associated with osteoarthritis or bursitis
  • Pain that is worse going down stairs — often patellofemoral pain (behind the kneecap)
  • Pain on the inner side (medial) — may suggest medial meniscus or MCL injury
  • Pain on the outer side (lateral) — often IT band syndrome or lateral meniscus
  • Pain at the front below the kneecap — patellar tendonitis
  • Pain all around the knee with swelling — possible arthritis or effusion

Self-Help Measures

  • RICE — Rest, Ice, Compression (a knee support), Elevation
  • Low-impact activity — swimming, cycling, walking (not running) during an acute episode
  • Weight management — even a 5% weight loss reduces knee pain significantly
  • Strengthening exercises — particularly quadriceps and gluteal muscles

When to See a Doctor

Seek medical assessment if your knee is significantly swollen, you cannot bear weight, you hear or feel a pop at the time of injury, pain is severe or worsening, or symptoms persist for more than 2–4 weeks despite self-care.

/library/sore-bottom-back.bodyHtml:
Overview

Pain at the very bottom of the back — in the lower lumbar and sacral region — is extremely common and can have a wide range of causes. The area includes the lowest vertebrae (L4, L5), the sacrum (the triangular bone at the base of the spine), and the sacroiliac joints (where the spine meets the pelvis). Pain here can radiate to the buttocks, hips, and down the legs.

Common Causes

  • Sacroiliac joint dysfunction — a common and often overlooked cause of low back and buttock pain
  • Lumbar disc herniation — a slipped disc pressing on the sciatic nerve (sciatica)
  • Lumbar spondylosis — age-related wear and tear of the lower spine
  • Piriformis syndrome — the piriformis muscle irritating the sciatic nerve in the buttock
  • Coccydynia — pain in the tailbone (coccyx), often after injury or prolonged sitting
  • Ankylosing spondylitis — inflammatory arthritis affecting the sacroiliac joints
  • Gluteal muscle tightness or strain

Treatment

  • Physiotherapy — targeted exercises for the lumbar spine and sacroiliac joint
  • Massage therapy
  • Anti-inflammatory medications
  • Heat and ice therapy
  • Posture and ergonomic advice
  • Sacroiliac joint injections if conservative measures fail

Posture Tips

Sitting for prolonged periods is a major aggravating factor. Take regular breaks from sitting, use a lumbar support cushion, and try to maintain a neutral spine position. Strengthening the core and gluteal muscles reduces strain on the lower back.

/library/access-to-work.question: Access to Work for arthritis: UK workplace support explained
/library/access-to-work.answer: Access to Work is a UK Government scheme that provides practical and financial support to people with a physical or mental health condition or disability, to help them get or stay in work. It can pay for things that are not covered by employers under their duty to make reasonable adjustments. The scheme is available to
/library/access-to-work.bodyHtml:
What is Access to Work?

Access to Work is a UK Government scheme that provides practical and financial support to people with a physical or mental health condition or disability, to help them get or stay in work. It can pay for things that are not covered by employers under their duty to make reasonable adjustments. The scheme is available to employees, self-employed people, and those starting a new job.

Who Can Apply?

You can apply if you:

  • Have a disability, long-term health condition (including rheumatoid arthritis, fibromyalgia, or other musculoskeletal conditions), or mental health condition
  • Are aged 16 or over
  • Are in paid employment or about to start work
  • Live and work in England, Scotland, or Wales

What Can Access to Work Fund?

  • Special equipment or adaptations to existing equipment
  • Changes to the working environment
  • Travel to and from work if you cannot use public transport
  • A support worker or job coach
  • Mental health support through an Employment Assistance Programme
  • Video relay services and communication support

How to Apply

You can apply online via the Government's Access to Work website, or by phone. A workplace assessment may be arranged to identify your needs. Grants awarded can vary significantly depending on individual circumstances.

Employer Responsibilities

Under the Equality Act 2010, employers must make reasonable adjustments for employees with a disability or long-term condition. Access to Work is designed to complement — not replace — these adjustments. Adjustments might include flexible working hours, ergonomic equipment, or modified duties.

Arthritis-specific workplace examples

People with arthritis often use Access to Work for sit-stand desks, ergonomic chairs, vertical mice, voice recognition software, parking closer to the entrance, or taxi fares during flares when public transport is not realistic. Self-employed people can also apply. Bring a short flare diary to any assessment so bad days are visible, not only good ones.

  • Dictation software when hand or wrist arthritis slows typing
  • Supportive seating and desk height for spinal or hip OA
  • Travel support when morning stiffness makes commuting unreliable

Next steps after you apply

While you wait for a decision, talk to your manager or HR about Equality Act reasonable adjustments, and ask occupational health for a workstation review if one is available. If benefits questions sit alongside work worries, use the PIP guide and evidence diary so you are not juggling blank forms alone.

faqs.q: What is Access to Work?
faqs.a: Access to Work is a UK government grant that can help pay for practical support if a disability or long-term health condition — including arthritis — affects your job. It complements, rather than replaces, your employer's Equality Act duty to make reasonable adjustments.

faqs.q: Who can apply for Access to Work with arthritis?
faqs.a: You can usually apply if you are 16 or over, live and work in England, Scotland or Wales, are in paid work or about to start, and have a long-term condition such as rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis or another musculoskeletal condition that affects how you do your job.

faqs.q: What can Access to Work pay for?
faqs.a: Common awards include specialist equipment or adaptations, changes to the working environment, travel to work if public transport is not manageable, a support worker or job coach, and some mental health support. Exact awards depend on individual assessment.

faqs.q: How do I apply for Access to Work?
faqs.a: Apply online via GOV.UK Access to Work or by phone. A workplace assessment may follow. You can apply before starting a new role or while already employed. Keep notes on flare days, tasks you struggle with, and equipment that already helps.

faqs.q: Does Access to Work replace reasonable adjustments?
faqs.a: No. Under the Equality Act 2010, employers must still consider reasonable adjustments such as flexible hours, extra breaks or modified duties. Access to Work is designed for support that goes beyond what is reasonable for the employer alone.

faqs.q: Can I claim PIP and Access to Work together?
faqs.a: Yes. PIP looks at daily living and mobility; Access to Work looks at workplace support. Many people use both. Start with our Benefits & PIP hub for claim prep, then use this page for workplace grants.

/library/naproxen-side-effects.title: Naproxen Side Effects | Living With Arthritis UK
/library/naproxen-side-effects.description: What to watch for when taking naproxen
/library/naproxen-side-effects.question: Naproxen Side Effects
/library/naproxen-side-effects.answer: Naproxen is well-tolerated by many people, but like all NSAIDs, it can cause side effects. The risk of side effects increases with higher doses and longer duration of use. This guide covers the most important side effects to be aware of.
/library/naproxen-side-effects.bodyHtml:
Overview

Naproxen is well-tolerated by many people, but like all NSAIDs, it can cause side effects. The risk of side effects increases with higher doses and longer duration of use. This guide covers the most important side effects to be aware of.

Common Side Effects (affect more than 1 in 100 people)

  • Indigestion and heartburn
  • Stomach pain or discomfort
  • Nausea
  • Constipation or diarrhoea
  • Headache
  • Dizziness
  • Drowsiness

Serious Side Effects (seek medical advice promptly)

  • Stomach ulcer — symptoms include persistent stomach pain, indigestion that doesn't improve, and loss of appetite
  • Gastrointestinal bleeding — dark, tarry, or bloody stools; vomiting blood (coffee-ground appearance) — seek emergency help immediately
  • Allergic reaction — rash, swelling of the face, lips, or throat, difficulty breathing — seek emergency help
  • Kidney problems — reduced urine output, swollen ankles, unusual tiredness
  • Liver problems — yellowing of skin or eyes (jaundice)
  • Heart attack or stroke symptoms — chest pain, sudden severe headache, facial drooping, arm weakness — call 999

How to Reduce Side Effect Risk

  • Always take with food or milk
  • Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time
  • Take a stomach-protecting medicine (PPI) if prescribed
  • Avoid alcohol
  • Stay hydrated
  • Inform your doctor of all other medications

/library/knee-support.title: Knee Support | Living With Arthritis UK
/library/knee-support.description: Braces and supports for knee pain and instability
/library/knee-support.question: Knee Support
/library/knee-support.answer: Knee supports range from simple elasticated sleeves to custom-made rigid braces. The right type depends on your condition and the level of support needed:
/library/knee-support.bodyHtml:
Types of Knee Supports

Knee supports range from simple elasticated sleeves to custom-made rigid braces. The right type depends on your condition and the level of support needed:

  • Compression sleeves — provide mild support and warmth; suitable for mild osteoarthritis, general knee aching, and swelling
  • Hinged knee braces — provide stability and limit range of motion; used after ligament injuries or surgery
  • Patellar tracking braces — help keep the kneecap in proper alignment; used for patellofemoral syndrome
  • Unloader (offloading) braces — shift weight away from the affected compartment; used for unicompartmental osteoarthritis
  • Custom orthopaedic braces — prescribed by a specialist and fitted individually for maximum support

Benefits of Knee Supports

  • Reduce pain during activity
  • Provide proprioceptive feedback (sense of joint position)
  • Reduce swelling through compression
  • Improve confidence and reduce fear of joint "giving way"
  • Allow continued activity during rehabilitation

Using a Knee Support Safely

  • Do not rely solely on a support — strengthening exercises remain essential
  • Ensure a proper fit — a poorly fitted support can worsen symptoms
  • Remove during sleep unless specifically advised otherwise
  • Check skin regularly for irritation or pressure sores

Where to Get a Knee Support

Knee supports are available from pharmacies, sports shops, and online. For complex knee conditions, ask for a physiotherapy referral for professional advice on the most appropriate support. Custom braces are available through UK healthcare orthotics departments or private providers.

/library/collagen-vs-glucosamine.description: Comparing the evidence, mechanisms and safety of two of the most asked-about joint supplements
/library/collagen-vs-glucosamine.question: Collagen vs Glucosamine for Arthritis
/library/collagen-vs-glucosamine.answer: Collagen and glucosamine are the two supplements people in the UK most often ask their GP and pharmacist about for joint pain. /library/collagen-vs-glucosamine.bodyHtml:
Why People Compare These Two

Collagen and glucosamine are the two supplements people in the UK most often ask their GP and pharmacist about for joint pain. Both are sold widely on the high street, both claim to support cartilage, and both are commonly used by people living with osteoarthritis. They work in different ways, the evidence behind each is different, and choosing between them often comes down to what your symptoms are, what you've already tried, and what your clinician advises.

How Each One Works

Glucosamine is a natural sugar produced by the body and a building block of cartilage. As a supplement it is usually sold as glucosamine sulfate or glucosamine hydrochloride. The theory is that supplementing it gives the body more raw material to maintain and repair cartilage.

Collagen is the most abundant structural protein in the body and a major component of cartilage, tendons and ligaments. Most joint-focused supplements use hydrolysed collagen (collagen peptides) or undenatured type II collagen. Hydrolysed collagen is thought to provide amino acids that support cartilage turnover, while undenatured type II collagen is thought to modulate the immune response that drives joint inflammation.

What the Evidence Says

Neither supplement reliably slows the progression of osteoarthritis. Both have a reasonable safety record. The clinical evidence is mixed for both, but here is the honest summary:

  • Glucosamine has the longer track record. Some trials — particularly of glucosamine sulfate at 1,500 mg daily — show modest reductions in knee pain and stiffness. Other large trials show no benefit over placebo. NICE does not currently recommend it for routine UK healthcare prescribing.
  • Combined glucosamine + chondroitin has shown small benefits in some moderate-to-severe knee osteoarthritis trials, though results are inconsistent.
  • Hydrolysed collagen (typically 10 g daily) and undenatured type II collagen (40 mg daily) have shown symptom improvements in several smaller trials, including reductions in pain scores and improved function — but the overall evidence base is thinner and shorter-term than for glucosamine.
  • Direct head-to-head comparisons of collagen vs glucosamine are limited. The few that exist suggest similar, modest effect sizes rather than one being clearly superior.

Safety and Who Should Be Careful

Both are generally well tolerated. Common side effects are mild and usually involve digestion — nausea, indigestion or loose stools. Important cautions:

  • Glucosamine is often made from shellfish, so people with a shellfish allergy should choose a vegetarian/vegan source or avoid it.
  • Glucosamine may interact with warfarin and other blood thinners — speak to your GP or pharmacist first.
  • People with diabetes should monitor blood sugar when starting glucosamine, as some studies have flagged small effects on glucose control.
  • Collagen supplements are usually derived from bovine, porcine, marine or chicken sources. Check the label if you avoid certain animal products or have allergies.
  • Neither supplement is recommended in pregnancy or breastfeeding without medical advice.

Which Should You Try First?

There is no universally best choice. A reasonable, pragmatic approach used by many UK clinicians is:

  • If your main problem is knee osteoarthritis with stiffness and you want the option with the longest evidence base, glucosamine sulfate 1,500 mg daily is a sensible 8–12 week trial.
  • If you have already tried glucosamine without benefit, or you have a shellfish allergy or take blood thinners, hydrolysed collagen 10 g daily or undenatured type II collagen 40 mg daily is a reasonable alternative to trial for 8–12 weeks.
  • Stop after the trial period if you notice no meaningful difference in pain, stiffness or daily function.
  • Neither replaces the core arthritis basics: weight management if needed, regular low-impact exercise, strength training around the affected joint, and pain relief agreed with your GP.

Bottom Line

Collagen and glucosamine sit in the same evidence tier — modest, inconsistent benefits for some people, no proven disease-modifying effect, and a good safety profile for most adults. Neither is a substitute for exercise, weight management or clinician-led treatment. Trial one for 8–12 weeks, judge by how you feel, and stop if it isn't helping.
